topics.name: End of life: hospice vs palliative

cfg.lastPassNote: Questions on the facts your class notes and study guide flag as exam topics (the leukemia, prostate, labs and staging items, the class PLQs and case studies). Shakiest first.

Q.q: A 62-year-old client reports fatigue, shortness of breath on stairs, and bleeding gums. The client has worked in an oil refinery since age 18 and has smoked for more than 40 years. Hgb is 9.4 g/dL and platelets are 97,000/mm³. Which part of the history places this client at the highest risk for leukemia?
o: Long-term benzene exposure from refinery work
Smoking for more than 40 years
Fatigue with shortness of breath on exertion
Bleeding gums
A hemoglobin of 9.4 g/dL
Q.w: Leukemia risk factors include genetic anomalies, Down syndrome, radiation, benzene or other chemical exposure, prior chemotherapy or radiation, and smoking. In this case the oil refinery is the benzene exposure and is identified as the highest risk factor. The low hemoglobin, low platelets, fatigue and bleeding gums are the effects of blasts crowding the marrow. They are findings the nurse assesses, not causes. (study guide, Ch 34 case)

x.Smoking for more than 40 years: Smoking is a listed leukemia risk factor, but it is not the highest risk in this history; the case names benzene as the highest.
x.Fatigue with shortness of breath on exer: This is a manifestation of anemia from a crowded marrow, not something that causes leukemia.
x.Bleeding gums: Bleeding gums are a sign of thrombocytopenia, not a cause of leukemia.
x.A hemoglobin of 9.4 g/dL: A low hemoglobin is a result of marrow crowding by blasts, not a risk factor.

m.Fatigue with shortness of breath on exer: mixes up a symptom with a risk factor
m.Bleeding gums: mixes up a symptom with a risk factor
m.A hemoglobin of 9.4 g/dL: mixes up a symptom with a risk factor

Q.q: The nurse is reviewing risk factors for leukemia with a client's family. Select all that apply.
o: Down syndrome
Prior chemotherapy or radiation
Benzene exposure
Presence of the Philadelphia chromosome in chronic myeloid leukemia
A diet high in red meat
Undescended testicle
Unopposed estrogen exposure
Q.w: Down syndrome raises leukemia risk about 10 to 30 times. Radiation, benzene and prior chemotherapy damage marrow stem cells. The Philadelphia chromosome, a 9;22 swap, is found in more than 90% of chronic myeloid leukemia. Each wrong option is the signature risk of a different cancer. (study guide, Ch 34)

x.A diet high in red meat: A diet high in red meat is a prostate cancer risk factor, not a leukemia risk factor.
x.Undescended testicle: Cryptorchidism is the greatest risk factor for testicular cancer.
x.Unopposed estrogen exposure: Unopposed estrogen is a main risk factor for uterine cancer.

m.A diet high in red meat: borrows a risk factor from another cancer
m.Undescended testicle: borrows a risk factor from another cancer
m.Unopposed estrogen exposure: borrows a risk factor from another cancer

Q.q: A 7-year-old child is admitted with fever, bone pain, and bruising. Testing confirms the most common childhood leukemia. Which type should the nurse expect the chart to list?
o: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia
Acute myeloid leukemia
Chronic myeloid leukemia
Chronic lymphocytic leukemia
Multiple myeloma
Q.w: Leukemias are named by the stem cell line and the speed of onset. AML and ALL have a sudden, acute onset, and ALL is the most common childhood leukemia. CML and CLL can be present for years before turning acute. Multiple myeloma is a separate plasma cell cancer. (study guide, Ch 34)

x.Acute myeloid leukemia: AML is acute but is tied to benzene, radiation and prior chemotherapy in adults; ALL is the most common childhood type.
x.Chronic myeloid leukemia: CML is chronic and marked by the Philadelphia chromosome, not the typical childhood form.
x.Chronic lymphocytic leukemia: CLL is chronic and can be present for years before it is found; it is not the common childhood leukemia.
x.Multiple myeloma: Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell cancer of older adults, not a leukemia.

m.Chronic myeloid leukemia: mixes up acute and chronic types
m.Chronic lymphocytic leukemia: mixes up acute and chronic types

Q.q: A client newly diagnosed with leukemia asks, “My white count is high, so why am I getting infections and bruising so easily?” Which response by the nurse is best?
o: “The extra white cells are immature blasts that cannot fight infection, and they crowd out the cells that make platelets and red cells.”
“Your body is making too many healthy neutrophils, and they are destroying your platelets.”
“The high count means your immune system is working extra hard to fight an infection.”
“Your chemotherapy has lowered your platelets and made you prone to infection.”
“Your spleen is destroying your blood cells faster than they can be made.”
Q.w: An unknown stimulus mutates a stem cell, which clones immature blasts that never mature and never die. The marrow, spleen and lymph tissue fill with blasts. The crowded marrow cannot make enough RBCs and platelets, so anemia and thrombocytopenia follow. The blasts cannot fight infection, so neutropenia and infections follow even when the count is high. (study guide, Ch 34)

x.\u201cYour body is making too many healt: The high count is from immature blasts, not healthy neutrophils, and they do not destroy platelets.
x.\u201cThe high count means your immune s: A high count in leukemia does not mean a stronger defense; the blasts are immature and useless.
x.\u201cYour chemotherapy has lowered your: The client has just been diagnosed; the problem comes from the leukemia itself, not from treatment.
x.\u201cYour spleen is destroying your blo: Splenomegaly can occur, but the main cause is marrow crowding by blasts.

m.\u201cYour body is making too many healt: thinks the extra cells are healthy
m.\u201cThe high count means your immune s: thinks a high WBC means strong defense

Q.q: The nurse is explaining the phases of chemotherapy for leukemia to a client. Place the phases in the order they are given.
o: Induction to bring the leukemia into remission
Consolidation to treat hidden disease
Maintenance to prevent relapse
Q.w: Induction aims to get remission. Consolidation treats leukemia cells that cannot be seen. Maintenance helps prevent relapse. Remission is not a cure, which is why therapy continues in phases. (study guide, Ch 34)

Q.q: The nurse reviews medications used for leukemia. Match each drug with its role.
o: Blocks the Bcr-Abl protein in CML
Targeted therapy used in CLL
Induction chemotherapy for AML
Growth factor that raises neutrophils
Q.w: Imatinib targets the Bcr-Abl abnormality of CML and ibrutinib is used in CLL. Daunorubicin plus cytarabine is the AML chemotherapy example. Filgrastim (G-CSF) raises neutrophils; the textbook says growth factors are generally not indicated in leukemia because they could fuel the disease, although the case patient received it, so ask your instructor how it will be tested. (study guide, Ch 34)

x.Blocks the Bcr-Abl protein in CML: Imatinib is a Bcr-Abl inhibitor given for CML; it does not treat CLL.
x.Targeted therapy used in CLL: Ibrutinib is the targeted agent listed for CLL.
x.Induction chemotherapy for AML: Daunorubicin plus cytarabine (Ara-C) is the AML example regimen.
x.Growth factor that raises neutrophils: Filgrastim is G-CSF, which raises neutrophils and can cause bone pain.

Q.q: A client with acute leukemia is receiving chemotherapy and has an absolute neutrophil count of 0.6 ×10³/mm³. Which medication group does the nurse expect to be ordered to lower the risk of infection?
o: Prophylactic antibiotics, antivirals and antifungals
Aspirin
Megestrol
Mesna
Allopurinol
Q.w: Chemotherapy causes myelosuppression, and severe neutropenia lets infection spread quickly. The case patient received prophylactic antibiotics, antivirals and antifungals along with blood products. Examples listed are levofloxacin or moxifloxacin, acyclovir and fluconazole. Each wrong option protects against a different chemotherapy problem. (study guide, Ch 34)

x.Aspirin: Aspirin inhibits platelets and raises bleeding risk; it does not prevent infection and is unsafe with thrombocytopenia.
x.Megestrol: Megestrol is used for anorexia, not infection prevention.
x.Mesna: Mesna protects the bladder from hemorrhagic cystitis.
x.Allopurinol: Allopurinol prevents high uric acid in tumor lysis; it does not prevent infection.

m.Megestrol: picks a drug for a different problem
m.Mesna: picks a drug for a different problem
m.Allopurinol: picks a drug for a different problem

Q.q: A client whose leukemia is in remission after induction chemotherapy tells the nurse, “I am relieved because this means I am cured.” The nurse recognizes that this statement is accurate.
o: True
False
Q.w: Remission means no detectable leukemia cells, but hidden disease can remain. That is why consolidation and maintenance follow induction. The true version is: remission is not the same as a cure, and treatment continues to prevent relapse. (study guide, Ch 34)

x.True: Marking True treats remission as a cure; the teaching need is that remission does not mean cure.

Q.q: A client with leukemia involving the brain asks why radiation to the brain and spine is planned along with chemotherapy. The nurse says it is because chemotherapy cannot cross the blood–brain barrier. The nurse's statement is accurate.
o: True
False
Q.w: Chemotherapy given by vein does not reach the central nervous system well. Radiation to the brain and spine treats leukemia cells that hide there. Some chemotherapy is also given intrathecally. (study guide, Ch 34)

x.False: Marking False denies that the blood–brain barrier blocks chemotherapy; this is the reason radiation is added.

Q.q: A client receiving chemotherapy for acute leukemia has a temperature of 101.8°F (38.8°C) and an ANC of 0.6 ×10³/mm³. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Notify the provider immediately so broad-spectrum IV antibiotics can be started
Give acetaminophen and recheck the temperature in 1 hour
Take a rectal temperature to confirm the reading
Encourage oral fluids and bed rest
Apply a cooling blanket
Q.w: In a chemotherapy client, fever is often the first and only sign of infection, and infection is the most common cause of death besides the disease itself. Myelosuppression with fever is treated aggressively with broad-spectrum antibiotics to prevent sepsis. A fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher is the trigger to call. Rectal temperatures and suppositories are avoided because rectal bacteria can enter the blood. (study guide, Ch 13 and Ch 34)

x.Give acetaminophen and recheck the tempe: Waiting delays treatment; fever may be the only sign of infection and needs antibiotics immediately.
x.Take a rectal temperature to confirm the: Rectal temperatures are never done in neutropenia because rectal bacteria can enter the blood.
x.Encourage oral fluids and bed rest: Fluids and rest are supportive but do not treat a possible infection, which is an emergency.
x.Apply a cooling blanket: Cooling lowers the temperature but does not treat the infection behind it.

m.Give acetaminophen and recheck the tempe: treats the fever, not the infection
m.Encourage oral fluids and bed rest: treats the fever, not the infection
m.Apply a cooling blanket: treats the fever, not the infection

Q.q: A client with leukemia has a platelet count of 19,000/mm³ after chemotherapy. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?
o: “I have an appointment to get my teeth cleaned this week.”
“I will go to the emergency department if I have a nosebleed that lasts more than 10 minutes.”
“I will go to the emergency department if my temperature reaches 102°F.”
“I will use an electric razor instead of a blade.”
Q.w: With platelets this low, dental cleaning can cause bleeding and bacteria can enter the blood, so it should be avoided. The other statements show correct bleeding and infection teaching: report a prolonged nosebleed and fever, and use an electric razor. After chemotherapy the first priority is infection, and platelets below 20,000 can bleed spontaneously. (study guide, Ch 34 case; class notes)

x.\u201cI will go to the emergency departm: This is correct teaching; a nosebleed lasting more than 10 minutes needs emergency care.
This is correct teaching; fever with neutropenia needs prompt treatment.
x.\u201cI will use an electric razor inste: This is correct teaching; an electric razor lowers the risk of cuts and bleeding.

Q.q: A client with newly diagnosed stage III lung cancer will start chemotherapy next week. The client asks the nurse when pain, shortness of breath and nausea can be managed by a specialty team. Which response is best?
o: “Palliative care can start now, at diagnosis, and it can continue along with chemotherapy.”
“Palliative care begins only after the cancer stops responding to treatment.”
“You must stop chemotherapy before palliative care can begin.”
“Palliative care is available only when a doctor estimates less than 6 months to live.”
Q.w: Palliative care relieves symptoms such as pain, dyspnea and nausea and improves quality of life for the client and family at any stage of a serious illness. It starts on the day of diagnosis and can go on while the client receives chemotherapy, radiation or surgery. Hospice is different: it is for the end of life and curative treatment stops. (study guide, Ch 26 and Other Topics)

x.\u201cPalliative care begins only after: Palliative care is not limited to the end of life; it starts at diagnosis.
x.\u201cYou must stop chemotherapy before: Palliative care can continue alongside chemotherapy, radiation and surgery; stopping curative treatment is a hospice requirement.
x.\u201cPalliative care is available only: The 6-month prognosis is the hospice rule, not the palliative rule.

m.\u201cPalliative care begins only after: thinks palliative means end of life only

Q.q: The nurse is teaching a family about hospice care for a client with end-stage cancer. Select all that apply.
o: The client has a prognosis of 6 months or less if the disease runs its usual course
Curative treatment is stopped and the focus is on comfort
Family support continues after the death, including bereavement
The client can leave hospice to restart curative treatment
Hospice can begin the day any serious illness is diagnosed
Chemotherapy and radiation are continued to cure the disease
Q.w: Hospice is for a client whose prognosis is 6 months or less. The client stops curative treatment and chooses comfort, dignity and a peaceful death, and the family receives support including bereavement. Hospice is usually provided at home but can be in a facility or nursing home, and a client can leave to restart curative care. All hospice is palliative, but not all palliative care is hospice. (study guide, Other Topics; standard content as labeled in the guide)

x.Hospice can begin the day any serious il: Starting at diagnosis describes palliative care; hospice is for the end of life.
x.Chemotherapy and radiation are continued: Hospice means the client stops curative treatment and chooses comfort care.

Q.q: A client with heart failure and several hospitalizations wants help with symptoms but still wants to try every treatment that might extend life. Which type of care fits this client's goals?
o: Palliative care
Hospice care
Hospice care with continued curative treatment
Care only after the client is declared terminal
Bereavement care only
Q.w: Palliative care is for anyone with a serious illness at any age or stage, and curative treatment can continue with it. Hospice is limited to the last months of life and replaces curative treatment with comfort care. The client's wish to keep treating points to palliative care. (study guide, Other Topics; standard content as labeled in the guide)

x.Hospice care: Hospice requires stopping curative treatment and a prognosis of 6 months or less; this client wants to keep treating.
x.Hospice care with continued curative tre: Hospice means the client stops curative treatment.
x.Care only after the client is declared t: Palliative care is open to anyone with a serious illness at any stage.
x.Bereavement care only: Bereavement support is a feature of hospice for the family after a death, not the client's present goal.

m.Care only after the client is declared t: thinks palliative means end of life only

Q.q: A nurse tells the daughter of a client with advanced cancer, “All hospice care is palliative, but not all palliative care is hospice.” The statement is accurate.
o: True
False
Q.w: Hospice is a form of care that aims at comfort, so everything it does is palliative. Palliative care is the wider umbrella: it treats symptoms such as pain, dyspnea and nausea at any stage and can run alongside chemotherapy, radiation or surgery. Because palliative care does not require the client to stop curative treatment, it is not always hospice. This is why “all hospice is palliative, but not all palliative care is hospice” is accurate. (study guide, Other Topics; Ch 26)

x.False: Marking False would mean hospice is not palliative or that palliative care is always hospice; neither is true.

Q.q: A nurse explains to a client with a new cancer diagnosis that palliative care and hospice are the same thing. The nurse's statement is accurate.
o: True
False
Q.w: Palliative care can begin at diagnosis and continue alongside curative treatment. Hospice is for the end of life and curative treatment stops. The true version is: palliative care is not the same as hospice. (study guide, Ch 26 and Other Topics)

x.True: Marking True treats the two as the same; palliative care is broader than hospice.

Q.q: A hospice nurse is assessing a client who is actively dying. Which findings suggest that death is near? Select all that apply.
o: Decreased oral intake and urine output
Mottled, cool extremities
Periods of apnea with Cheyne-Stokes breathing
Noisy secretions
A sudden increase in appetite and energy with a rising urine output
Warm, pink, well-perfused extremities
Q.w: As death nears, intake and urine output fall, the extremities become mottled and cool, and breathing becomes irregular with apnea and Cheyne-Stokes patterns. Noisy secretions, the “death rattle,” and a falling level of consciousness are also expected. Hearing is often the last sense lost, so the nurse keeps talking to the client. (study guide, Other Topics; standard content)

x.A sudden increase in appetite and energy: Intake and urine output fall as death nears; they do not rise.
x.Warm, pink, well-perfused extremities: Mottled, cool extremities are the sign of approaching death.

Q.q: A client in hospice care has dyspnea and pain at the end of life. Which action by the nurse is most consistent with comfort care?
o: Give the opioid as ordered on a regular schedule and provide mouth care and repositioning
Withhold opioids until the client's respiratory rate rises
Start curative chemotherapy to reduce the symptoms
Ignore the advance directive until the family arrives
Limit visitors to protect the client from emotional strain
Q.w: At the end of life the goal changes from cure to comfort, so symptoms are treated on a schedule rather than waiting for them to become severe. Opioids such as morphine relieve pain and the sensation of breathlessness, and they are given as ordered rather than withheld. Mouth care and repositioning prevent the discomfort that comes with reduced intake and immobility. The nurse also honors the advance directive and DNR order and supports the family. (study guide, Other Topics; standard content)

x.Withhold opioids until the client's resp: Opioids, including morphine for dyspnea, are given to keep the client comfortable.
x.Start curative chemotherapy to reduce th: Hospice means curative treatment has stopped.
x.Ignore the advance directive until the f: Advance directives and DNR orders are honored in end-of-life care.
x.Limit visitors to protect the client fro: Emotional and spiritual support for the client and family is part of nursing care.

Q.q: A 52-year-old client with estrogen receptor–positive breast cancer is starting tamoxifen. Which medication on the client's list should the nurse question?
o: A combined oral contraceptive
Acetaminophen as needed
A multivitamin
Calcium with vitamin D
A stool softener
Q.w: Estrogen-positive tumors are fed by estrogen, so oral contraceptives are questioned. Combined oral contraceptives also raise the risk of clots. Tamoxifen blocks estrogen at its receptor and is taken for 5 to 10 years. The other medications have no hormone effect. (study guide, Ch 65; Davis Table 65.3)

x.Acetaminophen as needed: Acetaminophen has no interaction with tamoxifen in these materials.
x.A multivitamin: A multivitamin is not a hormone and does not feed an estrogen-positive tumor.
x.Calcium with vitamin D: Calcium and vitamin D are not hormones and do not fuel the tumor.
x.A stool softener: A stool softener has no hormonal effect on the tumor.

Q.q: A client with breast cancer who takes tamoxifen reports depression and a new prescription for an SSRI. Which concern should the nurse raise with the provider?
o: SSRIs reduce how tamoxifen is metabolized
SSRIs increase the blood level of tamoxifen to a toxic range
SSRIs cause cardiotoxicity when combined with tamoxifen
SSRIs raise the risk of endometrial cancer with tamoxifen
SSRIs cause bone loss when combined with tamoxifen
Q.w: Tamoxifen is a selective estrogen receptor modulator that works only if the body converts it normally. SSRIs reduce tamoxifen metabolism, so the nurse tells the provider before the SSRI is started. Tamoxifen's own risks include DVT, PE, stroke, cataracts and endometrial cancer. (study guide, Ch 65; Davis Table 65.3)

x.SSRIs increase the blood level of tamoxi: The interaction lowers the tamoxifen's effect by reducing its metabolism; it does not cause toxicity.
x.SSRIs cause cardiotoxicity when combined: Cardiotoxicity is linked to trastuzumab, not to this combination.
x.SSRIs raise the risk of endometrial canc: Endometrial cancer risk comes from tamoxifen itself, not from SSRIs.
x.SSRIs cause bone loss when combined with: Bone loss is tied to aromatase inhibitors, and to tamoxifen in premenopausal clients, not to this SSRI interaction.

m.SSRIs increase the blood level of tamoxi: reverses the direction of the interaction

Q.q: The nurse reviews medications for breast cancer. Match each drug with its key nursing consideration.
o: Blocks estrogen at its receptor; avoid SSRIs
Blocks conversion of androgens to estrogen; risk of osteoporosis and fractures
For HER2-positive tumors; watch for cardiotoxicity
Immunotherapy given with chemotherapy before surgery; rash, diarrhea, thyroid problems
Q.w: Tamoxifen blocks estrogen at the receptor, while aromatase inhibitors stop androgens from becoming estrogen, so only the aromatase inhibitor carries the osteoporosis warning of this pair. Trastuzumab targets HER2 and can harm the heart. Pembrolizumab is immunotherapy. (study guide, Ch 65; Davis Table 65.3)

x.Blocks estrogen at its receptor; avoid S: Tamoxifen is a SERM taken for 5 to 10 years.
x.Blocks conversion of androgens to estrog: Aromatase inhibitors such as anastrozole, letrozole and exemestane work this way.
x.For HER2-positive tumors; watch for card: Trastuzumab (Herceptin) is a targeted antibody; it also causes fatigue, joint pain, diarrhea and fever.
x.Immunotherapy given with chemotherapy be: Pembrolizumab (Keytruda) is immunotherapy used with chemotherapy for high-risk triple-negative cancer.

Q.q: A 64-year-old male client has had a mastectomy for breast cancer. His tumor is estrogen receptor–negative and HER2-negative. Which order should the nurse question?
o: Antiestrogen therapy
Pain medication as needed
Dressing change using aseptic technique
Emptying and recording the surgical drain
Teaching about suture care
Q.w: Hormone therapy, such as tamoxifen, aromatase inhibitors or fulvestrant, works only on receptor-positive tumors. This tumor is receptor-negative, so antiestrogen therapy would not help and the order should be questioned. Trastuzumab and pertuzumab are for HER2-positive tumors. The other orders are routine post-operative care. (study guide, Ch 66; Davis table notes)

x.Pain medication as needed: Pain medication helps with coughing, deep breathing and walking after surgery.
x.Dressing change using aseptic technique: This is routine post-operative wound care.
x.Emptying and recording the surgical drai: Drain care and recording color and amount is expected after mastectomy.
x.Teaching about suture care: Suture care and signs of infection are part of expected teaching.

Q.q: A 66-year-old male client with a BRCA2 mutation finds a lump behind his nipple. Which statement about breast cancer in men is accurate for the nurse to include in teaching?
o: It is far less common than in women, and the small amount of breast tissue means it spreads easily to the nipple, skin and muscle
It is as common as breast cancer in women
Lumpectomy is the usual treatment because the tissue is small
Radiation is the main treatment
BRCA1 is far more common than BRCA2 in men
Q.w: Male breast cancer is about 100 times less common than in women and occurs mainly between ages 60 and 70. BRCA2 is the more common mutation. With so little tissue behind the nipple, the tumor is easier to feel but spreads to the nipple, skin and muscle early. Mastectomy is usual, with chemotherapy and hormone therapy only for receptor-positive tumors. (study guide, Ch 66)

x.It is as common as breast cancer in wome: It is about 100 times less common than in women.
x.Lumpectomy is the usual treatment becaus: Mastectomy is the usual treatment because there is so little tissue.
x.BRCA1 is far more common than BRCA2 in m: BRCA2 is the more common mutation in male breast cancer.

Q.q: A 22-year-old male client has a palpable lump behind the nipple and a strong family history of breast cancer. Which imaging does the nurse expect the provider to order first?
o: Ultrasound
Mammogram
Bone scan
PET scan
Chest x-ray
Q.w: In men the workup includes a clinical breast exam, then ultrasound if the client is under 25 years old or mammogram if 25 or older, and MRI. ER/PR and HER2 receptor tests then guide therapy. Bone scan, PET and chest x-ray look for metastasis. (study guide, Ch 66)

x.Mammogram: A mammogram is the choice for men age 25 and older; this client is under 25.
x.Bone scan: A bone scan looks for metastasis after the cancer is confirmed.
x.PET scan: PET scanning is used later to look for metastasis.
x.Chest x-ray: A chest x-ray is a staging test for spread, not the first imaging of a breast lump.

Q.q: A 45-year-old client is scheduled for a lumpectomy for early-stage breast cancer. The client asks what treatment will follow surgery. Which response by the nurse is correct?
o: “Breast conservation surgery is always followed by radiation, with chemotherapy first if it is indicated.”
“Radiation is not needed if the lumpectomy removed the whole tumor.”
“Radiation is given first to shrink the tumor, then surgery.”
“A mastectomy will be needed after the lumpectomy.”
“Only hormone pills are given after a lumpectomy.”
Q.w: Lumpectomy removes only the tumor plus a margin, and it is always followed by radiation. When chemotherapy is indicated the order is surgery, then chemotherapy, then radiation. For early disease lumpectomy and mastectomy are equivalent, so the client chooses. Endocrine therapy for 5 to 10 years is added for receptor-positive tumors. (study guide, Ch 65)

x.\u201cRadiation is not needed if the lum: Lumpectomy is always followed by radiation.
x.\u201cRadiation is given first to shrink: Chemotherapy, not radiation, is the usual neoadjuvant treatment to shrink a tumor before surgery.
x.\u201cA mastectomy will be needed after: Lumpectomy and mastectomy are equivalent for early disease; the patient chooses one.
x.\u201cOnly hormone pills are given after: Hormone therapy is added for receptor-positive tumors but does not replace radiation.

Q.q: A client has a 2 cm breast mass and the plan is chemotherapy before surgery, then mastectomy, then oral hormonal therapy. How should the nurse describe the oral hormonal therapy?
o: Adjuvant therapy given after the primary treatment
Neoadjuvant therapy given before the primary treatment
Palliative therapy to relieve symptoms
Primary therapy
Debulking therapy
Q.w: The timing words describe when a treatment is given relative to the definitive treatment, which here is the mastectomy. Neoadjuvant treatment comes before it and shrinks the tumor, which is why the chemotherapy in this plan is neoadjuvant. Adjuvant treatment comes after it and targets microscopic cells that may be left behind. Radiation and oral hormonal therapy after surgery are therefore adjuvant. (study guide, Ch 13 case and class PLQ)

x.Neoadjuvant therapy given before the pri: Neoadjuvant therapy is given before the definitive treatment; the chemotherapy in this plan is the neoadjuvant part.
x.Palliative therapy to relieve symptoms: The hormonal therapy is given to lower the risk from leftover cells, not to relieve symptoms.
x.Primary therapy: The primary therapy is the definitive treatment, here the surgery.
x.Debulking therapy: Debulking is partial removal of a tumor by surgery.

Q.q: A nurse reviews facts about breast cancer in situ lesions. Select all that apply.
o: Ductal carcinoma in situ is stage 0 and requires surgery
Lobular carcinoma in situ has no treatment and is followed with mammograms
Both lesions raise the risk of later invasive cancer
Lobular carcinoma in situ requires a mastectomy
Ductal carcinoma in situ needs no treatment
Q.w: DCIS is confined to the lining of the milk ducts, is stage 0, and requires surgery. LCIS is in the milk-producing lobules and is no longer considered cancer, so it has no treatment and the client is followed with mammograms and risk reduction. Both increase the chance of later invasive cancer. (study guide, Ch 65)

x.Lobular carcinoma in situ requires a mas: LCIS is no longer considered cancer and has no treatment; the focus is surveillance and risk reduction.

Q.q: A client returns to the unit after a mastectomy and axillary node removal. Which finding is the most concerning?
o: Bloody drainage saturating the dressing
Serosanguineous drainage in the surgical drain
Mild incisional pain rated 3 out of 10
A temperature of 99.0°F (37.2°C)
Q.w: Bloody drainage that saturates the dressing suggests bleeding and is the most concerning wound finding. Serosanguineous drainage is expected. Immediate post-operative complications include infection, wound dehiscence, pulmonary embolism and pneumonia. (study guide, Ch 65)

x.Serosanguineous drainage in the surgical: Serosanguineous drainage is expected after surgery.
x.Mild incisional pain rated 3 out of 10: Mild pain is expected and is treated, which also helps coughing and ambulation.
x.A temperature of 99.0\u00b0F (37.2\u00b0: This is not a fever and is not the most concerning finding.

Q.q: A client had radiation after a lumpectomy for left breast cancer. Which findings should the nurse monitor for as radiation effects? Select all that apply.
o: Redness and itching of the skin
Patchy desquamation
Breast swelling
A dry cough 6 weeks to 6 months later
Hot flashes and vaginal dryness
Skin rashes and flu-like symptoms
Q.w: Radiation irritates the skin, so the nurse monitors for redness, itching and patchy desquamation. The breast can swell for 6 to 18 months, and radiation pneumonitis causes a nonproductive cough 6 weeks to 6 months later. Late cardiac risk also exists. (study guide, Ch 65)

x.Hot flashes and vaginal dryness: These are effects of endocrine therapy, not radiation.

m.Hot flashes and vaginal dryness: mixes up radiation and hormone effects
m.Skin rashes and flu-like symptoms: mixes up radiation and immunotherapy effects

Q.q: A nurse teaches a client with breast cancer that monthly breast self-examination is the recommended screening method. The nurse's teaching is accurate.
o: True
False
Q.w: Breast self-exam is not recommended according to Chapter 65 and the slides. Screening is by mammography: annual from 45 to 54, then annual or every 2 years from age 55 while healthy. The true version is: breast self-exam is not recommended as screening. (study guide, Ch 65)

x.True: Marking True repeats the old teaching; the materials say breast self-exam is not recommended.

Q.q: A nurse tells a client after axillary node removal that the most common long-term effect is shoulder immobility and that arm swelling is called lymphedema. The nurse's statement is accurate.
o: True
False
Q.w: Removal of axillary nodes can cause lymphedema, arm swelling. Shoulder immobility, or frozen shoulder, is the most common long-term effect. Pain and scarring also occur. (study guide, Ch 65; class notes)

x.False: Marking False denies a long-term effect that is listed as the most common one.

Q.q: A client with leukemia has a platelet count of 45,000/mm³. Which action by the nurse is the priority?
o: Initiate bleeding precautions
Initiate neutropenic precautions
Increase iron-rich foods in the diet
Give a vitamin K injection
Encourage vigorous exercise
Q.w: Normal platelets are 150,000 to 450,000/mm³. Precautions start below 100,000, spontaneous bleeding is possible below 50,000 and especially below 20,000, and below 5,000 a fatal CNS or GI bleed can occur. A count of 45,000 calls for bleeding precautions such as a soft toothbrush, electric razor and no IM injections. (study guide, Ch 33 and cheat sheet)

x.Initiate neutropenic precautions: Neutropenic precautions are triggered by a low ANC, not by a low platelet count.
x.Increase iron-rich foods in the diet: Iron foods address iron deficiency anemia, not platelets.
x.Give a vitamin K injection: Vitamin K helps clotting factors, not a low platelet count.
x.Encourage vigorous exercise: Activity that risks falls and bumps raises the bleeding risk.

Q.q: Place these platelet counts in order from the highest to the lowest as the nurse considers bleeding risk.
o: 150,000/mm³: lower limit of normal
100,000/mm³: start bleeding precautions
50,000/mm³: spontaneous bleeding possible
20,000/mm³: platelets usually transfused
5,000/mm³: fatal CNS or GI bleed possible
Q.w: Platelets plug injured vessels, so the lower the count the less able the body is to stop bleeding. At 150,000 the count is at the lower limit of normal, and below it the client has thrombocytopenia. Precautions begin below 100,000, spontaneous bleeding becomes possible below 50,000, and platelets are usually transfused below 20,000 or before procedures. Below 5,000 a fatal central nervous system or GI bleed is possible. (study guide, Ch 33, Ch 34 and cheat sheet)

Q.q: A client receiving chemotherapy has a WBC differential showing an ANC of 400/mm³. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
o: The client has severe neutropenia and a high risk of infection
The client has thrombocytopenia and a high risk of bleeding
The client has anemia and needs iron
The client has a normal infection-fighting ability
The client has polycythemia
Q.w: A WBC differential shows the proportion of each type of white cell, and neutrophils are the first cells to arrive at an infection. Neutropenia is an ANC below 1,500, and 500 or below is severe and calls for neutropenic precautions. A fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher with neutropenia is treated aggressively. (study guide, Ch 13, Ch 33, Ch 34)

x.The client has anemia and needs iron: ANC measures neutrophils, not red cells or iron.
x.The client has a normal infection-fighti: An ANC below 1,500 is neutropenia and 500 or below is severe.
x.The client has polycythemia: Polycythemia is too many red cells.

Q.q: A client has a WBC differential showing many immature neutrophils, or bands. What does the nurse understand this left shift to mean?
o: The marrow is releasing immature cells to fight an active infection
The client has a chronic viral infection
The client has too many red blood cells
The client has normal marrow with stable cell counts
The client has low platelets
Q.w: In a left shift, immature neutrophils (bands) outnumber the normal amount, usually 3 to 5%. The marrow is pumping cells out early to fight infection or inflammation. Bands are not very effective at fighting infection. Bacterial infection raises neutrophils, while chemotherapy and radiation lower them. (study guide, Ch 33)

x.The client has a chronic viral infection: Left shift points to active bacterial-type infection or inflammation, not to a chronic viral illness.
x.The client has normal marrow with stable: Many bands means the marrow is being pushed to release cells early.
x.The client has low platelets: A left shift is a white-cell finding, not a platelet finding.

Q.q: A client's report lists reticulocytes of 4% of RBCs after a hemorrhage. What does the nurse understand this to mean?
o: The marrow is responding to blood loss by making more red cells
The marrow is not producing red cells
The client has leukemia
The client is dehydrated
The client has thrombocytopenia
Q.w: Reticulocytes are immature red cells released from the marrow, and they are larger than mature red cells. After a hemorrhage the marrow speeds up to replace lost cells, so more immature cells appear in the blood and the reticulocyte count rises above the normal 0.5 to 2.5%. In a marrow that is not producing, such as aplastic or pernicious anemia, the count is low instead. The count therefore tells the nurse how well the marrow is responding. (study guide, Ch 33)

x.The marrow is not producing red cells: A low reticulocyte count shows a marrow that is not producing, such as in aplastic or pernicious anemia.
x.The client has leukemia: Reticulocytes are immature red cells and do not point to leukemia.
x.The client is dehydrated: Dehydration raises the hematocrit but does not explain reticulocytes.
x.The client has thrombocytopenia: Reticulocytes are red cells, not platelets.

Q.q: A client with iron deficiency anemia has a serum iron test scheduled. The nurse explains that iron supplements must be held for at least [1] before the test, that the sample is best drawn in the [2], and that the total iron-binding capacity will be [3].
o: 24 hours
4 hours
2 weeks
morning
evening
afternoon
high
low
normal
Q.w: Iron supplements are avoided for at least 24 hours and an overnight fast is recommended. Serum iron is drawn in the morning because levels are lower in the evening. In iron deficiency TIBC is high because transferrin has many empty seats, while ferritin and transferrin saturation are low. (study guide, Ch 33 and class notes)

x.4 hours: Iron supplements are held at least 24 hours.
x.2 weeks: Two weeks is far longer than needed.
x.evening: Iron levels drop in the evening, so the sample is drawn in the morning.
x.low: TIBC is high in iron deficiency because there are many empty binding spots.
x.normal: TIBC is not normal in iron deficiency; it rises.

Q.q: A 25-year-old client with fatigue, pale nailbeds, a smooth red tongue and low ferritin has iron deficiency anemia. Which lunch choice shows the client understood diet teaching?
o: Roast beef, steamed spinach, tomato soup and orange juice
Cheese pizza with a glass of milk
Cereal with milk and a banana
Plain pasta with butter and a vanilla milkshake
Toast with margarine and tea
Q.w: Heme iron from red meat is paired with nonheme iron from spinach and vitamin C from tomatoes and orange juice, which increases absorption. Dairy and antacids reduce iron absorption. The class notes add that iron is taken with vitamin C on an empty stomach, not with milk. (study guide, Ch 34 and class notes)

x.Cheese pizza with a glass of milk: Dairy blocks iron absorption and this lunch has little iron.
x.Plain pasta with butter and a vanilla mi: This meal has little iron and the dairy blocks absorption.
x.Toast with margarine and tea: This meal has no heme iron, no vitamin C source, and no iron-rich vegetables.

Q.q: A client has iron deficiency anemia. Which laboratory findings should the nurse expect? Select all that apply.
o: Decreased serum ferritin
Increased total iron-binding capacity
Decreased transferrin saturation
Decreased MCV
Increased serum ferritin
Increased MCV
Increased transferrin saturation
Q.w: Iron is stored as ferritin and carried by transferrin, so when iron runs out the stores empty and ferritin, serum iron and transferrin saturation all fall. The transferrin carriers are left with many empty binding spots, which is why total iron-binding capacity rises. Without enough iron the marrow makes small, pale red cells, so the MCV and MCHC fall. The class slide gives ferritin below 100 for iron deficiency and the textbook gives below 10; ask your instructor which number will be tested. (study guide, Ch 33 and Ch 34)

x.Increased serum ferritin: Ferritin reflects iron stores and is low in iron deficiency.
x.Increased MCV: An increased MCV is macrocytic, as in B12 or folate deficiency; iron deficiency is microcytic.
x.Increased transferrin saturation: Transferrin saturation is always low in iron deficiency.

Q.q: The nurse reviews coagulation studies. Match each test with what it monitors.
o: Heparin, through the intrinsic pathway
Warfarin, through the extrinsic pathway
Platelet function
Abnormal platelet function from aspirin or von Willebrand disease
Q.w: The intrinsic pathway is monitored by PTT and the drug is heparin. The extrinsic pathway is monitored by PT and INR and the drug is warfarin. Your class notes list PT and PTT together for the intrinsic pathway, but the book and slide picture pair heparin with PTT, so PTT is the safe answer for heparin. (study guide, Ch 33 and class notes)

x.Warfarin, through the extrinsic pathway: PT and INR monitor warfarin; the INR goal is 2 to 3.
x.Platelet function: Bleeding time checks overall platelet function and is not done if platelets are under 75,000.
x.Abnormal platelet function from aspirin: Platelet aggregation is impaired in von Willebrand disease and with aspirin or NSAIDs.

Q.q: A nurse is preparing to collect blood for a CBC. Which tube should the nurse use?
o: Lavender (EDTA) tube
Light blue (sodium citrate) tube
Red top with no additive
Green (heparin) tube
Q.w: The tube additive decides which test can be run. A CBC needs whole blood that does not clot, so it goes in a lavender tube with EDTA. Clotting studies measure how fast plasma clots, so they use sodium citrate, which is reversible, and the tube must be filled completely to keep the blood-to-additive ratio right. The tourniquet comes off as soon as blood flows because leaving it on for more than a minute falsely raises the RBC, Hgb and Hct. (study guide, Ch 33)

x.Light blue (sodium citrate) tube: Sodium citrate tubes are used for PT, INR and PTT.
x.Red top with no additive: The CBC is drawn in an EDTA tube.
x.Green (heparin) tube: A heparin tube is not the tube listed for the CBC.

m.Light blue (sodium citrate) tube: mixes up the CBC and coagulation tubes

Q.q: A nurse teaches a student that a client with iron deficiency anemia will typically show microcytic and hypochromic red cells. The nurse's statement is accurate.
o: True
False
Q.w: Hemoglobin needs iron, and the amount of hemoglobin determines how large and how dark a red cell is. When iron is lacking the marrow makes cells with less hemoglobin, so they are smaller (a low MCV, microcytic) and paler (a low MCHC, hypochromic). Lead poisoning produces the same picture. Large cells, by contrast, point to a lack of B12 or folate. (study guide, Ch 33)

x.False: Marking False would label iron deficiency as macrocytic; macrocytic cells point to B12 or folate deficiency.

Q.q: A nurse tells a student that a platelet count of 100,000/mm³ is the level at which spontaneous bleeding becomes possible. The nurse's statement is accurate.
o: True
False
Q.w: At 100,000 bleeding precautions start. Spontaneous bleeding becomes possible below 50,000, and especially below 20,000. The true version is: precautions start at 100,000, and spontaneous bleeding is possible below 50,000. (study guide, Ch 33 and cheat sheet)

x.True: Marking True moves the spontaneous-bleeding threshold up to 100,000.

Q.q: A 68-year-old client who has smoked two packs a day for decades is told the biopsy shows small cell (oat cell) lung cancer. Which statement by the nurse is accurate?
o: “This type grows quickly and spreads to other organs early, so surgery is not the main treatment.”
“This is the most common type, making up about 85% of lung cancers.”
“If it is found early, the 5-year survival is good.”
“It includes adenocarcinoma, squamous cell and large cell types.”
“Surgery is used primarily for this type when it has not spread.”
Q.w: Smoking causes mutations that turn off the controls on cell growth, and the two lung cancer groups behave very differently once that happens. Small cell cancer is about 15% of cases, grows fast and spreads to other organs early, so removing the tumor does not cure it and surgery is not the main treatment. Its outlook is poor at any stage: only 5 to 10% survive 5 years, and your class notes give a life expectancy of 6 months to 1 year. Non-small cell cancer is about 85%, has three cell types, grows more slowly, and has a good 5-year survival if found early, so surgery is used when there is no metastasis. (study guide, Ch 26 and class notes)

x.\u201cThis is the most common type, maki: About 85% of lung cancers are non-small cell; small cell is about 15%.
x.\u201cIf it is found early, the 5-year s: Good early-stage survival describes non-small cell cancer; small cell has a poor outlook at any stage.
x.\u201cIt includes adenocarcinoma, squamo: Those three cell types make up non-small cell cancer.
x.\u201cSurgery is used primarily for this: Surgery is used primarily for non-small cell cancer without metastasis.

m.\u201cIf it is found early, the 5-year s: gives small cell the non-small cell outlook

Q.q: The nurse reviews the features of non-small cell lung cancer with a nursing student. Select all that apply.
o: It makes up about 85% of lung cancers
Its cell types are adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma and large cell carcinoma
Surgery is used primarily when there is no metastasis
The 5-year survival is good when it is found at an early stage
It grows quickly and spreads early to other organs
Life expectancy is typically 6 months to 1 year
It is also called oat cell cancer
Q.w: Non-small cell lung cancer is the larger and slower group with three cell types, and early-stage disease has a good 5-year survival. Surgery is the preferred treatment when there is no metastasis. The wrong options all describe small cell, the faster and poorer-outlook type. (study guide, Ch 26 and class notes)

x.It grows quickly and spreads early to ot: That describes small cell lung cancer.
x.Life expectancy is typically 6 months to: That is the class figure for small cell lung cancer.
x.It is also called oat cell cancer: Oat cell is another name for small cell lung cancer.

Q.q: A 70-year-old client with known lung cancer reports a new headache and bone pain. Which finding does the nurse recognize as suggesting metastasis?
o: Headache and bone pain
A new cough that does not go away
Hoarseness
Frequent pneumonia or bronchitis
Hemoptysis
Q.w: Early lung cancer often has no symptoms. As it advances, cues include a new or changed cough, hemoptysis, shortness of breath, wheezing, hoarseness, chest pain, weight loss and frequent pneumonia. Headache and bone pain suggest metastasis to the brain and bone; common sites are brain, bone, adrenal gland and the other lung. Bone pain also prompts a calcium check. (study guide, Ch 26 and Ch 13)

x.A new cough that does not go away: A new or changing cough is a presenting cue of lung cancer itself, not a sign of spread.
x.Hoarseness: Hoarseness is a presenting symptom of lung cancer.
x.Frequent pneumonia or bronchitis: This is a presenting cue from airway obstruction and infection.
x.Hemoptysis: Hemoptysis comes from small vessels rupturing in the lung.

m.A new cough that does not go away: treats a presenting cue as a sign of spread
m.Hoarseness: treats a presenting cue as a sign of spread
m.Frequent pneumonia or bronchitis: treats a presenting cue as a sign of spread
m.Hemoptysis: treats a presenting cue as a sign of spread

Q.q: A client with suspected lung cancer is scheduled for a PET scan. The client asks what the test shows. Which response by the nurse is best?
o: “It shows areas of high metabolic activity, such as rapidly dividing cancer cells, rather than the structure of the lung.”
“It shows the structure of the airways so the provider can take a tissue sample.”
“It is a small chest incision to look at the nodes in the middle of the chest.”
“It identifies the type of tumor cells in the mucus you cough up.”
“It looks only for fractures of the ribs.”
Q.w: A PET scan detects how metabolically active tissue is, and rapidly dividing cancer cells are very active, so they light up as hot spots (glucose must be controlled before the scan). That is why PET reveals metabolism rather than anatomy. Structure and tissue are shown by other tests: chest x-ray and CT find the lesion, sputum cytology may identify tumor cells, bronchoscopy allows a biopsy of the airways, and mediastinoscopy is a surgical incision to view and biopsy the mediastinum. (study guide, Ch 26)

x.\u201cIt shows the structure of the airw: Airway structure and tissue sampling describe bronchoscopy.
x.\u201cIt looks only for fractures of the: PET looks at metabolism; bone and abdominal scans look for metastasis.

m.\u201cIt identifies the type of tumor ce: mixes up PET and sputum cytology

Q.q: The nurse reviews lung cancer surgery and testing with a client. Match each procedure with its description.
o: Removes one entire lobe when the cancer is localized to that lobe
Removes the entire lung when cancer is spread diffusely through it
Removes a small section of a lobe for cancer in one small area
A surgical incision to view and biopsy the mediastinum
Q.w: Surgery is preferred if there is no metastasis. The extent of cancer decides the operation: a small area gets a wedge resection, one lobe gets a lobectomy, and a diffusely spread cancer needs a pneumonectomy. Mediastinoscopy is used to biopsy the nodes. (study guide, Ch 26)

x.A surgical incision to view and biopsy t: This is mediastinoscopy, a diagnostic test rather than a treatment.

Q.q: The nurse explains the WHO pain ladder used for cancer pain. Place the steps in order from mild to severe pain.
o: Step 1: a nonopioid such as acetaminophen or an NSAID
Step 2: a moderate opioid such as codeine, hydrocodone or oxycodone plus a nonopioid
Step 3: a strong opioid such as morphine or fentanyl plus a nonopioid
Q.w: The ladder matches the strength of the drug to the intensity of the pain. A nonopioid is first, and it is kept at every step because it adds pain relief and lets the opioid dose stay lower. When pain is moderate a weaker opioid is added, and when it is severe a strong opioid such as morphine or fentanyl is used. Doses are given around the clock rather than on demand, so that the level of relief stays steady and pain peaks are avoided. (study guide, Ch 26 and Ch 11)

Q.q: A client with lung cancer has dyspnea and a SpO₂ of 87% on room air. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Raise the head of the bed to semi-Fowler's position and apply oxygen to keep the SpO₂ at 90% or higher
Lay the client flat to rest
Offer a large meal to improve strength
Encourage the client to walk the hall
Wait and recheck the SpO₂ in 1 hour
Q.w: A SpO₂ below 90% means poor gas exchange. Oxygen is given to keep the SpO₂ at 90% or higher, and semi-Fowler's allows full lung expansion and better oxygenation. Small frequent meals with supplements avoid pressure on the diaphragm, and pain, anti-anxiety and bronchodilator medications help the client relax and open the airway. (study guide, Ch 26)

x.Lay the client flat to rest: Lying flat reduces lung expansion; semi-Fowler's allows full expansion and better oxygenation.
x.Offer a large meal to improve strength: A large meal pushes on the diaphragm; small frequent meals with supplements are better.
x.Encourage the client to walk the hall: Activity increases oxygen demand; the client has activity intolerance.
x.Wait and recheck the SpO\u2082 in 1 hour: A SpO₂ below 90% is a significant oxygenation problem that needs action now.

Q.q: A nurse sees a coworker about to clamp the chest tube of a client who had a lobectomy, to move the client to a chair. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Intervene, because the chest tube should never be clamped; air or fluid can build up and cause a tension pneumothorax
Allow it, because clamping prevents air from entering the pleural space
Allow it for a short time only
Disconnect the tube from the drainage system to make moving easier
Ask the client to hold the tube while standing
Q.w: After lobectomy or pneumonectomy the nurse keeps the chest tube system closed, watches the water-seal chamber, and never clamps the tube. Persistent bubbling in the water-seal chamber means an air leak. Excess bloody drainage suggests a bleed and cloudy drainage suggests infection. (study guide, Ch 26)

x.Allow it, because clamping prevents air: Clamping traps air and fluid in the pleural space and can cause a tension pneumothorax.
x.Allow it for a short time only: The rule is to never clamp the chest tube.
x.Disconnect the tube from the drainage sy: The system must stay closed to prevent air leaks.
x.Ask the client to hold the tube while st: This does not address the unsafe clamping and the closed system must be maintained.

m.Allow it for a short time only: believes a brief clamp is safe

Q.q: A client who had a lobectomy yesterday has continuous bubbling in the water-seal chamber of the chest tube drainage system. The nurse recognizes this as which finding?
o: An air leak in the system
Normal re-expansion of the lung
Excess bloody drainage
Infection of the pleural space
Atelectasis
Q.w: The water-seal chamber works as a one-way valve: air leaves the pleural space and bubbles through the water, but cannot come back. A brief bubble when the client coughs is expected, but bubbling that never stops means air is entering the system continuously. That points to a leak somewhere in the drainage system or the lung. The nurse also checks vital signs for hypotension or tachycardia from blood loss, breath sounds for atelectasis, and the suture line for infection. (study guide, Ch 26)

x.Normal re-expansion of the lung: Normal drainage does not cause persistent bubbling in the water-seal chamber.
x.Excess bloody drainage: Bleeding is judged by the amount and color of drainage, not by bubbling.
x.Infection of the pleural space: Cloudy drainage, not bubbling, suggests infection.
x.Atelectasis: Atelectasis is suspected when breath sounds are diminished or absent.

Q.q: A nurse tells a client with a 30 pack-year smoking history who quit 4 years ago that a yearly low-dose CT is recommended for all adults over age 65, regardless of smoking history. The nurse's statement is accurate.
o: True
False
Q.w: There is no general screening guideline for lung cancer. A yearly low-dose CT is for high-risk clients: current smokers or those who quit within 15 years, with at least a 20 pack-year history. The true version is that screening is for this high-risk group only. (study guide, Ch 13 and Ch 26)

x.True: Marking True extends screening to everyone over 65; it is limited to high-risk clients.

Q.q: A client newly diagnosed with lung cancer asks when palliative care can begin. The nurse answers that it begins at diagnosis to manage pain, dyspnea and nausea. The nurse's answer is accurate.
o: True
False
Q.w: Palliative care is built around the client's symptoms and quality of life, not around how long the client is expected to live. Lung cancer causes pain, dyspnea and nausea from the time it is diagnosed, so the help is needed from day one. For that reason palliative care starts at diagnosis and continues alongside chemotherapy or radiation. It is not the same as hospice, which is for the end of life. (study guide, Ch 26 Connection Check)

x.False: Marking False delays palliative care to the end of life, which is the hospice timing.

Q.q: The nurse reviews the CRAB criteria used to support a diagnosis of multiple myeloma. Select all that apply.
o: Calcium above 11.5 mg/dL
Creatinine above 2 mg/dL
Hemoglobin below 10 g/dL
Lytic bone lesions or pathologic fractures
Platelets above 450,000/mm³
Philadelphia chromosome present
Reed–Sternberg cells on biopsy
Q.w: Each letter of CRAB comes from a way the abnormal plasma cells damage the body. Lytic bone lesions release calcium, which causes hypercalcemia and also bone disease with fractures. Excess light chains injure the kidney, which causes renal insufficiency, and the crowded marrow causes anemia. Plasma cells of 10% or more in the marrow and an M protein in serum or urine complete the picture. (study guide, Ch 34)

x.Platelets above 450,000/mm\u00b3: A high platelet count is not part of CRAB.
x.Philadelphia chromosome present: The Philadelphia chromosome is linked to chronic myeloid leukemia.

m.Reed\u2013Sternberg cells on biopsy: mixes up myeloma and Hodgkin lymphoma

Q.q: A client with multiple myeloma has Bence Jones protein in the urine. Why does the nurse monitor BUN and creatinine closely?
o: The excess light chains are toxic to the kidneys
The M protein lowers the blood pressure and starves the kidneys
Bisphosphonates always cause kidney failure
The tumor grows directly inside the kidney
Low platelets cause bleeding into the kidneys
Q.w: One clone of plasma cells overgrows the marrow and pumps out monoclonal immunoglobulin, the M protein. Excess light chains, called Bence Jones protein in the urine, are directly toxic to the kidney, and calcium released from lytic bone lesions adds stones and renal injury. The nurse watches BUN, creatinine, intake and output, and serum and urine calcium. (study guide, Ch 34)

x.The M protein lowers the blood pressure: The harm comes from light chains and calcium, not from low blood pressure.
x.Bisphosphonates always cause kidney fail: The kidney damage in myeloma comes from light chains and hypercalcemia, not from treatment.
x.The tumor grows directly inside the kidn: Myeloma is a plasma cell cancer of the marrow; the kidney is harmed by what the cells make.
x.Low platelets cause bleeding into the ki: Bleeding is not the cause of the kidney damage here.

Q.q: A client with multiple myeloma reports sudden severe back pain and new numbness in both legs. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Assess motor and sensory function in the legs and notify the provider immediately
Apply a heating pad to the back and reassess in the morning
Encourage the client to walk to loosen the back
Give an extra dose of the calcium supplement
Document the finding and continue routine care
Q.w: Myeloma destroys bone, so sudden severe pain, or pain in a new spot, especially the back, may mean a pathologic fracture or vertebral collapse. Spinal cord compression causes numbness, tingling and motor changes. The nurse assesses and reports at once, and teaches the client to report sudden severe pain and any change in sensation or movement. (study guide, Ch 34)

x.Apply a heating pad to the back and reas: Sudden severe pain with numbness may be a fracture or spinal cord compression, which cannot wait.
x.Encourage the client to walk to loosen t: Walking could worsen a vertebral fracture or cord compression.
x.Give an extra dose of the calcium supple: Hypercalcemia is a risk in myeloma, so extra calcium is harmful.
x.Document the finding and continue routin: These are emergency warning signs that must be reported.

m.Give an extra dose of the calcium supple: forgets the client is at risk for hypercalcemia

Q.q: A client with multiple myeloma is admitted with hypercalcemia and bone pain. Which nursing interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Encourage fluids to dilute calcium and protect the kidneys
Encourage ambulation as tolerated
Position the client for comfort
Monitor serum and urine calcium, BUN and creatinine
Restrict fluids to lower urine output
Maintain strict bed rest
Offer a calcium supplement for bone strength
Q.w: Fluids dilute calcium and protect the kidneys from stones and light chains. Walking as tolerated gives weight bearing that builds bone and helps prevent DVT. Positioning for comfort eases nerve compression, and monitoring calcium, BUN and creatinine tracks kidney damage. Bisphosphonates, chemotherapy and pain medication are given as ordered. (study guide, Ch 34 and class notes)

x.Restrict fluids to lower urine output: Fluids are encouraged to dilute the calcium and prevent stones.
x.Maintain strict bed rest: Weight bearing builds bone and prevents DVT and deconditioning.
x.Offer a calcium supplement for bone stre: The client already has too much calcium in the blood from bone breakdown.

Q.q: A client with multiple myeloma is prescribed ibandronate (Boniva). Which purpose should the nurse include in teaching?
o: It reduces bone breakdown, which lowers calcium and the risk of fractures
It replaces the clotting factors the client is missing
It kills the abnormal plasma cells directly
It raises the blood calcium to strengthen bone
It lowers uric acid and prevents tumor lysis
Q.w: Bisphosphonates slow bone breakdown, so fewer fractures occur and calcium falls. Examples include ibandronate (Boniva), pamidronate and zoledronate. Long-term use with bisphosphonates or denosumab can cause osteonecrosis of the jaw. (study guide, Ch 34 and class notes)

x.It replaces the clotting factors the cli: Replacing factors is the treatment for hemophilia.
x.It kills the abnormal plasma cells direc: Chemotherapy such as thalidomide, lenalidomide or bortezomib attacks the cancer cells.
x.It raises the blood calcium to strengthe: The drug lowers calcium by slowing bone breakdown.
x.It lowers uric acid and prevents tumor l: Allopurinol and rasburicase are used for uric acid.

m.It kills the abnormal plasma cells direc: mixes up bone drugs and chemotherapy

Q.q: A nurse reviews the signs of hypercalcemia in a client with multiple myeloma. Which finding should the nurse expect?
o: Constipation, muscle weakness and polyuria
Peaked T waves on the ECG
Dilutional hyponatremia with seizures
Hypotension, tachycardia and hives
Ribbon-like stools with vomiting
Q.w: Hypercalcemia from bone breakdown causes confusion or lethargy, muscle weakness, polyuria and dehydration, constipation and nausea, bradycardia and heart block. Your class notes add tingling and burning sensation. Fluids dilute the calcium. (study guide, Ch 13, Ch 34 and class notes)

x.Peaked T waves on the ECG: Peaked T waves are a sign of hyperkalemia, as in tumor lysis syndrome.

Q.q: A nurse tells a client newly diagnosed with multiple myeloma that the disease is an incurable B-cell cancer of plasma cells. The nurse's statement is accurate.
o: True
False
Q.w: A single clone of plasma cells, which are mature B cells that make antibodies, overgrows the marrow and cannot be fully removed. Because the clone is spread through the marrow and bones, treatment aims to control the disease and its complications rather than cure it. That is why the nurse focuses on pain control, calcium and kidney protection, infection and fracture prevention. Chemotherapy, dexamethasone, bisphosphonates and an autologous stem cell transplant are options. (study guide, Ch 34)

x.False: Marking False would tell the client the disease is curable; it is described as incurable.

Q.q: A nurse tells a woman of childbearing age who is starting thalidomide or lenalidomide for multiple myeloma that these drugs are safe to take during pregnancy. The nurse's statement is accurate.
o: True
False
Q.w: These two drugs interfere with the normal development of a fetus, so they are called teratogenic. A woman who becomes pregnant while taking them could have a baby with serious defects. The safe teaching is that a woman of childbearing age needs reliable contraception, and the same two-forms-of-birth-control rule appears for methotrexate in the class case. Claiming they are safe in pregnancy is therefore wrong. (study guide, Ch 34; class notes)

x.True: Marking True would expose a fetus to a teratogenic drug.

Q.q: A 71-year-old client with metastasis to the bone from prostate cancer says, “I never had any trouble urinating.” Which explanation by the nurse is correct?
o: Prostate tumors usually grow at the edges of the gland, so they do not block urine flow early
The tumor grows inside the urethra but is too small to block it
The client's bladder muscle compensated for the blockage
Prostate cancer never affects urination
The metastasis to the bone relieved the pressure on the urethra
Q.w: Prostate cancer is slow growing and asymptomatic until it is advanced. Because the tumors grow on the periphery of the gland, they do not obstruct urine flow early and go unnoticed until they cause pain. That is how a client can have late-stage disease with no urinary trouble. It spreads to lymph nodes, bone, rectum and bladder. (study guide, Ch 66 and class PLQ)

x.The tumor grows inside the urethra but i: Tumors grow on the periphery of the gland, away from the urethra.
x.The client's bladder muscle compensated: There was no early blockage to compensate for.
x.Prostate cancer never affects urination: Urinary symptoms appear when the cancer advances.
x.The metastasis to the bone relieved the: Metastasis does not relieve urinary obstruction.

m.The tumor grows inside the urethra but i: places the tumor at the urethra

Q.q: A 56-year-old client has a PSA of 4.6 ng/mL and an enlarged prostate on digital rectal exam. Which statement by the nurse is accurate?
o: “A PSA of 4 or higher needs further evaluation, and a biopsy confirms the diagnosis.”
“A PSA this high confirms that you have prostate cancer.”
“A PSA below 4 means cancer is not possible.”
“PSA rises only with cancer, not with infection or an enlarged prostate.”
“The next step is a radical prostatectomy.”
Q.w: PSA of 4 ng/mL or higher needs further assessment, and the diagnosis requires a needle biopsy, then a Gleason score and TNM staging. PSA has high sensitivity but low specificity, so infection and enlargement can raise it. A large palpable prostate plus a high PSA needs workup. (study guide, Ch 66 and Ch 13)

x.\u201cA PSA this high confirms that you: PSA has high sensitivity but low specificity and cannot confirm cancer; biopsy does.
x.\u201cA PSA below 4 means cancer is not: No PSA value guarantees there is no cancer.
x.\u201cPSA rises only with cancer, not wi: Prostatitis and BPH also raise PSA, which is why it cannot tell BPH from cancer.
x.\u201cThe next step is a radical prostat: Treatment decisions follow biopsy, Gleason score and staging.

m.\u201cA PSA below 4 means cancer is not: treats a low PSA as a guarantee

Q.q: A client has returned to the unit after a radical prostatectomy. Which complications should the nurse monitor for? Select all that apply.
o: Erectile dysfunction
Urinary incontinence
Infection, such as fever, increasing pain, swelling or redness
Bleeding with clots in the urine
Hearing loss from ototoxicity
Lymphedema of the arm
Dry cough from pneumonitis
Q.w: Impotence is the most expected complication after radical prostatectomy and nerve-sparing surgery only tries to protect the erection nerves. Urinary incontinence, infection, and bleeding with clots are also watched for. The nurse manages bladder irrigation to clear clots, gives stool softeners to avoid straining, and uses aseptic wound care. (study guide, Ch 66; class notes)

x.Hearing loss from ototoxicity: Ototoxicity is a chemotherapy effect of testicular cancer drugs such as cisplatin.
x.Lymphedema of the arm: Arm lymphedema follows axillary node removal in breast cancer.

m.Hearing loss from ototoxicity: borrows a complication from another cancer
m.Lymphedema of the arm: borrows a complication from another cancer
m.Dry cough from pneumonitis: borrows a complication from another cancer

Q.q: A client has continuous bladder irrigation after prostate surgery. The nurse explains that the irrigation is used to do what?
o: Clear blood clots so the catheter stays open
Treat a urinary tract infection
Lower the PSA level
Dissolve bladder stones
Deliver chemotherapy to the bladder
Q.w: After prostate surgery bleeding and clots can block urine flow. Bladder irrigation clears the clots and keeps the urine light pink. Stool softeners prevent straining, which could start bleeding. (study guide, Ch 66)

x.Treat a urinary tract infection: Infection is treated with antibiotics; irrigation clears clots.
x.Dissolve bladder stones: Stones are not the purpose of irrigation after this surgery.

Q.q: After a prostatectomy a client is ordered a daily stool softener. The client asks why it is needed. Which response by the nurse is best?
o: “It prevents straining, which could cause bleeding at the surgical site.”
“It lowers your PSA level.”
“It treats the infection in your prostate.”
“It helps the radioactive seeds pass.”
Q.w: After prostate surgery there are fresh wounds and vessels in and around the bladder neck. Straining to pass a hard stool raises pressure in the pelvis and can restart bleeding or dislodge clots, so the nurse prevents it. A stool softener keeps the stool soft so the client does not strain. It works together with bladder irrigation, which clears clots, and aseptic wound care. (study guide, Ch 66)

x.\u201cIt lowers your PSA level.\u201d: Stool softeners have no effect on PSA.
x.\u201cIt treats the infection in your pr: A stool softener does not treat infection.
x.\u201cIt helps the radioactive seeds pas: Seeds are implanted in brachytherapy, not passed after prostatectomy.

Q.q: A client is having permanent radioactive seeds placed through the perineum for early prostate cancer. Which statement by the client indicates understanding of safety teaching?
o: “I will avoid sex for 2 weeks and then use a condom to protect my partner from radiation.”
“I can resume unprotected intercourse after one day.”
“The seeds will be taken out after a week.”
“The seeds are placed through my abdomen under general anesthesia.”
“The seeds are for cancer that has spread to my bones.”
Q.w: Brachytherapy places radioactive seeds permanently through the perineum, as an outpatient procedure, for cancer that has not spread outside the prostate. The client avoids sex for 2 weeks and then uses a condom. Radiation and brachytherapy can cause incontinence and impotence. (study guide, Ch 66)

x.\u201cI can resume unprotected intercour: The teaching is no sex for 2 weeks, then a condom.
x.\u201cThe seeds will be taken out after: Brachytherapy seeds for prostate cancer are placed permanently.
x.\u201cThe seeds are placed through my ab: They are placed through the perineum as an outpatient procedure.
x.\u201cThe seeds are for cancer that has: Brachytherapy is for cancer that has not spread outside the prostate.

Q.q: A nurse is caring for a client who has a radioactive implant for prostate cancer. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Minimize contact time and wear proper, thicker PPE
Wear no protective equipment because the client is not radioactive
Wear only regular gloves
Spend as much time at the bedside as possible
Let the family handle all body-fluid care without teaching
Q.w: Brachytherapy places the radiation source inside or next to the tumor, so the client can expose others to radiation. The nurse therefore minimizes contact and wears proper, thicker PPE. This differs from external beam radiation, where the machine delivers the dose and the client is not radioactive. Body fluids of a brachytherapy client may carry radioactive material, so the family is taught the precautions too. (study guide, Ch 13, Ch 66 and class notes)

x.Wear no protective equipment because the: Not being radioactive is true for external beam therapy; with brachytherapy the nurse limits exposure.
x.Wear only regular gloves: Proper, thicker PPE is needed to minimize radiation exposure.
x.Spend as much time at the bedside as pos: Time near the source should be limited.
x.Let the family handle all body-fluid car: Brachytherapy clients may eliminate radioactive material in body fluids, so the family is taught too.

m.Wear no protective equipment because the: applies the external beam rule to brachytherapy

Q.q: A client with prostate cancer reports fever, malaise and a rising white blood cell count after treatment. Which principle should guide the nurse's care?
o: Infection is the most likely cause
This is an expected response to the tumor
This indicates hemorrhage
This indicates the cancer has become stage IV
This is an adverse effect of a stool softener
Q.w: Cancer and its treatment weaken the body's defenses, and surgery or catheters add entry points for bacteria. Fever, malaise and a rising WBC are the body's response to an infection, so infection is the most likely cause and is checked first. After prostate surgery infection also shows as increasing pain, swelling, redness, drainage and nausea or vomiting. The nurse reports these findings and uses aseptic wound care. (study guide, Ch 66 and class PLQ)

x.This is an expected response to the tumo: Fever with a high WBC in a cancer client points first to infection.
x.This indicates hemorrhage: Hemorrhage shows with bleeding, low blood pressure and a rising heart rate.
x.This indicates the cancer has become sta: Staging cannot be judged from a fever.
x.This is an adverse effect of a stool sof: A stool softener does not cause fever.

Q.q: A client is scheduled for a nerve-sparing radical prostatectomy. Which statement by the client indicates understanding of the surgery?
o: “The surgery tries to protect the nerves that control erection, but impotence is still likely.”
“The surgery guarantees I will keep normal erections.”
“The surgery removes only the outer layer of the prostate.”
“The surgery will prevent any problem with urine control.”
“The surgery is done with radioactive seeds placed through the skin.”
Q.w: Radical prostatectomy removes the prostate and seminal vesicles, with or without pelvic nodes, and almost always results in impotence. The nerve-sparing approach attempts to keep intact the nerves that control erection. Incontinence, infection, bleeding and clots are other complications to watch for. (study guide, Ch 66)

x.\u201cThe surgery guarantees I will keep: Radical prostatectomy almost always results in impotence; nerve-sparing only tries to protect the nerves.
x.\u201cThe surgery removes only the outer: Radical prostatectomy removes the prostate and seminal vesicles, with or without pelvic nodes.
x.\u201cThe surgery will prevent any probl: Urinary incontinence is a possible complication.

Q.q: A nurse tells a client that African American men have a higher incidence of prostate cancer and about twice the mortality. The nurse's statement is accurate.
o: True
False
Q.w: The risk of prostate cancer is not the same in every group. African American men, and Caribbean men of African ancestry, have a higher incidence and about twice the mortality of other men. Because of this the screening conversation starts earlier, at age 45 rather than 50. The nurse should know the disparity when discussing PSA and rectal exam screening. (study guide, Ch 66 and Ch 13)

x.False: Marking False denies a documented disparity.

Q.q: A nurse teaches a client that benign prostatic hyperplasia is an early stage of prostate cancer. The nurse's statement is accurate.
o: True
False
Q.w: BPH is an enlargement of the gland from changes such as dihydrotestosterone buildup, and it squeezes the urethra. It is a benign process and does not turn into cancer. A man can have both conditions at the same time, which is why PSA cannot separate them and why a biopsy is used to confirm cancer. The statement that BPH is an early stage of cancer is therefore false. (study guide, Ch 66)

x.True: Marking True treats BPH as a pre-cancer.

Q.q: A nurse is reviewing risk factors with a 58-year-old client. Which finding is a nonmodifiable risk factor for cancer?
o: A genetic predisposition such as a BRCA1 mutation
A sedentary lifestyle
A diet low in vegetables
Smoking one pack a day
Heavy alcohol use
Q.w: Age and genetics cannot be changed, and 5 to 10% of cancers come from known genetic syndromes such as BRCA1/2, p53 and FAP. Lifestyle factors such as inactivity, poor diet, smoking and alcohol are modifiable. The nine risk factor categories are carcinogens, environment, hormones, genetics, lifestyle, infectious disease, medications, immune status and nutrition. Carcinogen exposure is the most common risk factor. (study guide, Ch 13)

Q.q: A 38-year-old client reports an HPV infection, multiple sexual partners, early sexual contact and tobacco use. For which cancer is the client at increased risk?
o: Cervical cancer
Ovarian cancer
Uterine cancer
Breast cancer
Prostate cancer
Q.w: Cervical cancer risk factors include HPV, multiple partners, early sexual contact, tobacco use and long-term oral contraceptive use. HPV is the cause: nearly all cervical cancers test positive. Each other option has its own typical risk set. (study guide, Ch 13 Table 13.2 and Ch 65)

x.Ovarian cancer: Ovarian risk is tied to BRCA1/2, nulliparity and not breastfeeding.
x.Uterine cancer: Uterine risk is tied to estrogen, obesity, PCOS and tamoxifen.
x.Breast cancer: Breast risk is tied to early menarche, late menopause, BRCA and obesity.
x.Prostate cancer: Prostate cancer occurs in men and is tied to age, family history and pesticides.

Q.q: The nurse reviews risk factors from the cancer risk table. Match each cancer with a risk factor.
o: H. pylori infection
Hepatitis B or C
Undescended testicle
Asbestos exposure
Q.w: Each cancer has exposures that damage its own organ, and the table pairs them. H. pylori inflames the stomach lining, alcohol and viral hepatitis injure the liver, and an undescended testicle is a developmental problem of the testis. Asbestos and tobacco damage the airway lining. Knowing which exposure hits which organ lets the nurse match a client's history to the cancer. (study guide, Ch 13 Table 13.2)

x.H. pylori infection: H. pylori is listed with gastric cancer.
x.Hepatitis B or C: Hepatitis A, B or C and alcohol are listed for liver cancer.
x.Undescended testicle: Cryptorchidism is the greatest risk for testicular cancer.
x.Asbestos exposure: Tobacco, asbestos, coal, soot, tar, pollution and wood dust are listed for lung cancer.

Q.q: A client with a BRCA2 mutation asks which cancers, besides breast and ovarian, are linked to this gene. Which response by the nurse is correct?
o: Pancreatic cancer, prostate cancer and melanoma
Lung cancer and mesothelioma
Colon and rectal cancer
Bladder and kidney cancer
Cervical and vulvar cancer
Q.w: BRCA genes normally repair DNA, so a mutation lets damaged cells survive and multiply. BRCA1 raises the risk of breast and ovarian cancer. BRCA2 raises those too and adds pancreatic and prostate cancer and melanoma, and it is the more common mutation in male breast cancer. The other options belong to other exposures such as tobacco, asbestos or HPV. (study guide, Ch 13 and Ch 66)

x.Lung cancer and mesothelioma: Those are tied to tobacco and asbestos.
x.Colon and rectal cancer: Colon cancer risk is tied to polyps, alcohol, obesity and inflammatory bowel disease in these materials.
x.Bladder and kidney cancer: Those are tied to tobacco, pesticides and solvents.

Q.q: A nurse reviews red flags for hereditary cancer. Select all that apply.
o: Multiple primary tumors in the same client
Bilateral tumors in paired organs
