Cancer at a younger age than usual
A tumor in a sex not usually affected, such as male breast cancer
Two or more first-degree relatives with the same cancer
A single tumor found at the usual age in a client with no family history
One distant relative with a different cancer
Q.w: A hereditary syndrome is a mutation that is present in every cell from birth, so it shows up as cancer that appears earlier, more often, or in unusual places. That explains the red flags: multiple primaries, bilateral tumors in paired organs, a younger-than-usual age, a tumor in the sex not usually affected, and two or more first-degree relatives with the same cancer. A single tumor at the usual age with no family history does not fit the pattern. These clients are referred for genetic counseling. (study guide, Ch 13)

x.A single tumor found at the usual age in: This pattern does not suggest a hereditary syndrome.
x.One distant relative with a different ca: The flag is two or more first-degree relatives with the same cancer.

Q.q: The nurse is planning cancer prevention activities. Match each activity with its level of prevention.
o: Primary prevention
Secondary prevention
Tertiary prevention
Q.w: Primary prevention stops cancer before it starts: risk factor modification, immunization and chemoprevention. Secondary prevention finds it early by screening. Tertiary prevention limits harm after diagnosis. (study guide, Ch 13 and class notes)

x.Primary prevention: Primary prevention modifies risk: avoiding carcinogens, immunization and chemoprevention.
x.Secondary prevention: Secondary prevention is screening for early detection such as breast, cervical, colon and prostate screening.
x.Tertiary prevention: Tertiary prevention reduces morbidity and mortality once the disease is diagnosed.

r: Managing side effects after a cancer diagnosis

Q.q: The nurse teaches the CAUTION warning signs. The A stands for a [1] that does not heal, the T stands for a [2] or lump, and a sign lasting more than [3] should be evaluated.
o: sore
rash
cough
thickening
tenderness
tingling
2 weeks
2 days
6 months
Q.w: CAUTION is a memory aid for the changes that early cancers cause in tissue. Each letter names a change: bowel or bladder habits, a sore that does not heal, unusual bleeding or discharge, a thickening or lump, indigestion or difficulty swallowing, an obvious change in a wart or mole, and a nagging cough or hoarseness. Benign causes usually settle in days, so a sign that lasts more than 2 weeks needs evaluation. (study guide, Ch 13)

x.rash: The A stands for a sore that does not heal.
x.cough: A nagging cough is the N.
x.tenderness: The T stands for thickening or lump.
x.tingling: Tingling is not part of CAUTION.
x.2 days: The guideline is more than 2 weeks.

Q.q: A nurse teaches a client that carcinogen exposure is the most common risk factor for cancer and that risks are cumulative. The nurse's teaching is accurate.
o: True
False
Q.w: A carcinogen damages DNA, and cancer develops when damage builds up faster than the cell and immune system can repair or remove it. For that reason one exposure rarely causes cancer; multiple exposures plus genetic mutations that the immune system misses are what lead to it. The risks are cumulative over a lifetime. Carcinogen exposure is therefore the most common risk factor. (study guide, Ch 13)

x.False: Marking False denies that carcinogen exposure is the most common risk.

Q.q: A nurse tells a client that most cancers come from known genetic syndromes such as BRCA1 and BRCA2. The nurse's statement is accurate.
o: True
False
Q.w: Inherited mutations such as BRCA1/2, p53 and FAP are present from birth and raise the risk sharply, but they are uncommon. They account for only 5 to 10% of cancers. Most cancers come from exposures and age, which add damage over time. The statement that most cancers come from known syndromes is therefore false. (study guide, Ch 13)

x.True: Marking True overstates the share of cancers caused by inherited syndromes.

Q.q: A 24-year-old client has painless neck swelling, drenching night sweats and generalized itching. A lymph node biopsy confirms Hodgkin lymphoma. Which finding on the biopsy defines this type?
o: Reed–Sternberg cells
The Philadelphia chromosome
Bence Jones protein
Heinz bodies
An M protein spike
Q.w: Hodgkin lymphoma is defined by Reed–Sternberg cells, giant lymphocytes, and has a better survival rate than non-Hodgkin lymphoma. It peaks in young adulthood and again after 55 and is linked to Epstein–Barr virus. A lymph node biopsy is definitive. (study guide, Ch 34)

x.The Philadelphia chromosome: The Philadelphia chromosome is found in chronic myeloid leukemia.
x.Bence Jones protein: Bence Jones protein is a finding of multiple myeloma.
x.Heinz bodies: Heinz bodies are seen with G6PD deficiency.
x.An M protein spike: The M protein is a finding of multiple myeloma.

Q.q: The nurse assesses a client with suspected Hodgkin lymphoma. Which findings are expected? Select all that apply.
o: Painless swelling of cervical, axillary or inguinal lymph nodes
Drenching night sweats
Unexplained weight loss
Generalized itching with scratch marks
A dry cough that is worse when lying flat
Tender, warm lymph nodes with a sore throat
A smooth red tongue and spoon-shaped nails
Severe back pain with high calcium and high creatinine
Q.w: Lymphoma causes painless lymph node swelling. B symptoms are low-grade fevers, drenching night sweats and unexplained weight loss. Itching is common in Hodgkin lymphoma, and a dry cough worse lying flat suggests a mediastinal mass that can compress the trachea. Fatigue is not a B symptom. (study guide, Ch 34 and Ch 13)

x.Tender, warm lymph nodes with a sore thr: Painful, tender nodes point to infection; lymphoma nodes are painless.
x.A smooth red tongue and spoon-shaped nai: These are signs of iron deficiency anemia.

Q.q: A client with Hodgkin lymphoma reports facial and arm swelling, shortness of breath, chest pain and trouble swallowing. Which complication does the nurse suspect?
o: Superior vena cava syndrome
Tumor lysis syndrome
Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone
Bowel obstruction
Leukostasis
Q.w: Enlarged nodes or a mediastinal mass can squeeze the soft-walled superior vena cava so blood cannot return from the upper body. This is an emergency with dyspnea, edema of the face, neck and arms, and chest pain. Treatment includes chemotherapy or radiation and corticosteroids. (study guide, Ch 13 and Ch 34)

x.Tumor lysis syndrome: Tumor lysis causes hyperkalemia, hypocalcemia and renal failure after treatment.
x.Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic h: SIADH causes hyponatremia with confusion and seizures.
x.Bowel obstruction: Bowel obstruction causes vomiting, distention and ribbon-like stools.
x.Leukostasis: Leukostasis occurs in leukemia with a very high WBC.

Q.q: A client with lymphoma reports back pain followed by numbness and tingling in both legs. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Perform a neurologic assessment and notify the provider immediately
Offer a back massage and reassess later
Position the client for comfort and reassess in the morning
Document the findings and continue the plan of care
Q.w: Spinal cord compression is a lymphoma emergency. Back pain and sensory changes come before motor weakness, and bowel and bladder dysfunction is late. Radiation and corticosteroids give rapid relief. (study guide, Ch 13 and Ch 34)

x.Offer a back massage and reassess later: Back pain with sensory change may be spinal cord compression, an emergency.
x.Position the client for comfort and reas: The delay could allow permanent paralysis.
x.Document the findings and continue the p: These are warning signs that need an urgent report.

Q.q: A client with lymphoma has a serum calcium of 12 mg/dL, confusion and polyuria. Which intervention should the nurse anticipate?
o: IV fluids to dilute the calcium
Restricting oral fluids
A calcium supplement
A dose of heparin
Q.w: In lymphoma, bone involvement releases calcium into the blood, and high calcium makes the kidneys lose water. That causes polyuria and dehydration, and the high level affects the brain and the heart, causing confusion and heart block. A calcium above 11 mg/dL is an emergency. IV fluids replace the losses and dilute the calcium, so they are the expected intervention. (study guide, Ch 34)

x.Restricting oral fluids: Fluids are encouraged to dilute the calcium.
x.A calcium supplement: The calcium is already too high.

Q.q: A client with lymphoma has involvement of two lymph node regions on the same side of the diaphragm. Which stage does the nurse document?
o: Stage II
Stage I
Stage III
Stage IV
Q.w: Lymphoma staging follows how far the disease has traveled through lymph tissue. Stage I is a single node, stage II is two or more nodes on the same side of the diaphragm, and stage III is nodes on both sides. Stage IV means organs are involved as well as nodes. The letters E for extranodal and S for spleen add detail. (study guide, Ch 34)

x.Stage I: Stage I is a single node.
x.Stage III: Stage III means nodes on both sides of the diaphragm.
x.Stage IV: Stage IV means organs plus nodes.

Q.q: A client with painless lymph node enlargement has a CBC, chest x-ray and CT scan. Which test is definitive for diagnosing lymphoma?
o: Lymph node biopsy
CBC
Chest x-ray
Serum uric acid and LDH
PET scan
Q.w: Blood tests and imaging show that something is wrong and how far it has spread, but they cannot show what the cells are. Uric acid and LDH rise from high cell turnover, and the CBC can show marrow involvement. Only tissue can prove lymphoma, so a lymph node biopsy is definitive. A bone marrow biopsy or lumbar puncture is added if marrow or CNS involvement is suspected. (study guide, Ch 34)

x.CBC: A CBC shows marrow involvement but does not diagnose lymphoma.
x.Chest x-ray: Imaging shows extent, not the diagnosis.
x.Serum uric acid and LDH: These are raised from high cell turnover but are not diagnostic.
x.PET scan: A PET scan helps staging and does not confirm the diagnosis.

Q.q: A client with lymphoma is about to start chemotherapy. Which information is most essential for the nurse to teach?
o: Neutropenic and bleeding precautions
Preparing for surgery to remove the tumor
Preparing for a splenectomy
How to avoid all fluids to reduce night sweats
Limiting rest to speed recovery
Q.w: Chemotherapy is the primary treatment for lymphoma, with radiation and immunotherapy. It lowers white cells and platelets, so neutropenic and bleeding precautions are the most essential teaching. The nurse also teaches the infection risk, frequent rest, nutrition, symptoms to report and fertility preservation. (study guide, Ch 34 and class PLQ)

x.Preparing for surgery to remove the tumo: Surgery to remove the tumor is not typical; chemotherapy is the primary treatment.
x.How to avoid all fluids to reduce night: Fluids replace losses from fever and sweats and dilute calcium.
x.Limiting rest to speed recovery: The client should rest often and keep the treatment schedule.

Q.q: A nurse tells a client with lymphoma that a dry cough that is worse lying flat may mean a mediastinal mass that can compress the airway. The nurse's statement is accurate.
o: True
False
Q.w: Lymph nodes in the chest can enlarge into a mediastinal mass. When the client lies flat the mass presses on the trachea and irritates it, which causes a dry persistent cough that worsens when lying down. Because the airway can be compressed, this sign is a warning of an airway risk and needs prompt evaluation. The nurse should not dismiss the cough. (study guide, Ch 34)

x.False: Marking False ignores a warning sign of airway compression.

Q.q: A nurse teaches that generalized itching with scratch marks is more common in non-Hodgkin lymphoma than in Hodgkin lymphoma. The nurse's teaching is accurate.
o: True
False
Q.w: Hodgkin lymphoma often causes generalized itching, and scratching leaves excoriation. The skin changes are one of the recognizable features that help separate it from non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Both lymphomas cause painless node swelling and B symptoms. The true teaching is that itching is more typical of Hodgkin lymphoma. (study guide, Ch 34)

x.True: Marking True gives the symptom to the wrong lymphoma.

Q.q: A client with stage III breast cancer classified as T3, N2, M1 is being taught about the staging. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?
o: “I am relieved that the cancer is still local.”
“The T tells me about the size of my tumor.”
“The N tells me about the lymph nodes that are affected.”
“The M1 tells me the cancer has spread to other parts of my body.”
Q.w: TNM stands for tumor size (T), number of lymph nodes involved (N) and presence of metastasis (M). M1 means metastasis is present, so the cancer is not local. A client who feels relieved that it is still local needs more teaching. (study guide, Ch 13 and class PLQ)

x.\u201cThe T tells me about the size of m: This is correct; T is the size of the tumor.
x.\u201cThe N tells me about the lymph nod: This is correct; N is the number of lymph nodes involved.
x.\u201cThe M1 tells me the cancer has spr: This is correct; M1 means metastasis is present.

Q.q: A client has been told her breast cancer is stage III and asks what that means. Which description by the nurse is best?
o: A large tumor or locally advanced cancer that may be in nearby lymph nodes
A small tumor with no obvious spread outside the organ
A tumor that has invaded deeper tissues or local lymph nodes
A cancer that has spread to other organs
Q.w: Staging puts the extent of disease on a scale from small and local to spread. Stage I is small with no obvious spread outside the organ, stage II invades deeper tissue or local nodes, stage III is large or locally advanced and possibly in local nodes, and stage IV has metastasized to other organs. Your class notes recorded a different answer for this case (spread to the lymph and blood systems), but the textbook definition is the one the case answer key supports, so confirm with your instructor. (study guide, Ch 13 and class PLQ)

x.A cancer that has spread to other organs: Spread to other organs is stage IV.

m.A cancer that has spread to other organs: mixes up stage III and IV

Q.q: The nurse reviews cancer classification terms. Match each term with its meaning.
o: Size of the primary tumor
Number of lymph nodes involved
Presence of distant spread, yes or no
How differentiated the cells look under the microscope
Q.w: Staging and grading answer two different questions. Staging asks how big the tumor is and how far it has spread, using T for size, N for the number of lymph nodes and M for metastasis. Grading asks how differentiated the cells look under the microscope. Poorly differentiated cells no longer look like the parent cell, so they are harder to treat and more aggressive. (study guide, Ch 13)

x.How differentiated the cells look under: Grading describes differentiation; poorly differentiated cells are more aggressive.

Q.q: A client's breast cancer is 3.5 cm with no lymph node involvement and no metastasis. Which stage does the nurse expect on the chart?
o: Stage IIA
Stage IA
Stage IB
Stage IIB
Stage IIIA
Q.w: Breast sizes to remember are 2 cm or less (stage I), 2 to 5 cm (stage II), and over 5 cm (stage IIB or III). A 2 to 5 cm tumor with no nodes is stage IIA. Nodes: 4 to 8 for IIIA, up to 9 for IIIB, 10 or more for IIIC. (study guide, Ch 65)

x.Stage IA: Stage IA is a tumor up to 2 cm with no nodes.
x.Stage IB: Stage IB is no tumor or under 2 cm with small node involvement.
x.Stage IIB: Stage IIB is 2 to 5 cm with nodes, or over 5 cm with no nodes.
x.Stage IIIA: Stage IIIA is over 5 cm with nodes, or any size with 4 to 8 nodes.

m.Stage IA: mixes up the breast size cutoffs
m.Stage IB: mixes up the breast size cutoffs
m.Stage IIB: mixes up the breast size cutoffs
m.Stage IIIA: mixes up the breast size cutoffs

Q.q: A client's prostate cancer is described as T2. Which description does the nurse understand?
o: The tumor is confined to the prostate
The tumor cannot be felt and is not seen on ultrasound
The tumor is locally extensive beyond the gland
The tumor has invaded neighboring organs
Q.w: In the prostate system the T number shows how far the tumor has grown locally. T1 cannot be felt on exam, T2 is confined to the prostate, T3 is locally extensive, and T4 invades neighboring organs. A Gleason grade describes the cells separately: two sites are graded 1 to 5 and added, for a maximum of 10. A higher score means more poorly differentiated cells. (study guide, Ch 66)

Q.q: A client's pathology report lists a prostate Gleason score of 9. Which statement by the nurse is accurate?
o: “A higher score means poorly differentiated cells and a worse prognosis, and 10 is the maximum.”
“A score of 9 means a 90% chance of cure.”
“A score of 9 means the cancer is stage IX.”
“A lower score means more aggressive cancer.”
“The score measures how large the tumor is.”
Q.w: Two sites in the biopsy are each graded from 1 to 5 and the grades are added. Grade 1 is well differentiated, looks nearly normal, and has the best prognosis. Grade 5 is poorly differentiated and has a poor prognosis. A total of 9 out of a maximum of 10 therefore means poorly differentiated cells and a worse outlook. The score is a grade, not a stage or a cure percentage. (study guide, Ch 66)

x.\u201cA score of 9 means a 90% chance of: The score is a grade of the cells, not a cure percentage.
x.\u201cA score of 9 means the cancer is s: Stages run I to IV; Gleason is a grade.
x.\u201cThe score measures how large the t: Size is the T in TNM; Gleason measures how differentiated the cells are.

Q.q: A client's ovarian cancer has spread to the peritoneum and lymph nodes. Which FIGO stage does the nurse expect?
o: Stage III
Stage I
Stage II
Stage IV
Q.w: Ovarian cancer is staged from what the surgeon finds, because it is not biopsied beforehand. The FIGO stages follow how far the disease has spread from the ovaries: stage I is limited to the ovaries and stage II extends into the pelvis. Stage III means the peritoneum and/or lymph nodes are involved, and stage IV is distant spread. Spread to the peritoneum and nodes is therefore stage III. (study guide, Ch 65)

x.Stage I: Stage I is limited to the ovaries.
x.Stage II: Stage II extends to the pelvis.

Q.q: A pathology report describes a client's tumor cells as poorly differentiated. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
o: The cells look unlike the parent cell, and the cancer is more aggressive and harder to treat
The tumor is small and has not spread
The tumor has spread to lymph nodes
The cells look like the parent cell and respond well to treatment
Q.w: Altered differentiation means the cell no longer looks or acts like the parent cell. Well differentiated cells look like the parent cell, while poorly differentiated cells are more aggressive and harder to treat. This is the basis of grading, which is separate from staging. (study guide, Ch 13)

x.The tumor is small and has not spread: Differentiation describes how cells look, not size or spread.
x.The tumor has spread to lymph nodes: Node spread is the N in TNM.

Q.q: A nurse tells a client with leukemia that all hematologic malignancies are considered stage IV at diagnosis because they involve the whole body from the start. The nurse's statement is accurate.
o: True
False
Q.w: Solid tumors start in an organ and spread outward, so size and spread give a stage. Leukemia, lymphoma and multiple myeloma start in blood-forming or lymph tissue, which circulates through the whole body. They therefore involve the body from the start and are classed as stage IV at diagnosis. The statement is accurate. (study guide, Ch 13)

x.False: Marking False would stage a leukemia like a small local solid tumor.

Q.q: A nurse teaches that the grade of a tumor describes how far the cancer has spread in the body. The nurse's teaching is accurate.
o: True
False
Q.w: Grade and stage measure different things. Grade describes how differentiated the cells look under the microscope, and poorly differentiated cells are more aggressive. Stage describes size, lymph node involvement and metastasis, which is how far the cancer has spread. The statement mixes the two up and is false. (study guide, Ch 13)

x.True: Marking True mixes up grade and stage.

Q.q: A 25-year-old client had her first Pap smear at age 21 with normal results. Primary HPV testing is not available at the clinic. Which services should the nurse expect at today's visit?
o: A breast exam, a pelvic exam and a Pap smear without HPV cotesting
A Pap smear with an HPV cotest
An HPV test alone every year
No screening until age 30
An immediate colposcopy
Q.w: Cervical screening starts at 21 with a Pap every 3 years, and HPV testing is only a reflex test if atypical cells are found in ages 21 to 29. Primary HPV screening may start at 25 and repeat every 5 years. The Ch 13 table groups ages 25 to 65, while Ch 65 starts at 21; the Ch 65 schedule is used here. (study guide, Ch 65 and class PLQ)

x.A Pap smear with an HPV cotest: HPV cotesting is not used before age 30.
x.An HPV test alone every year: HPV testing alone is primary screening every 5 years and is not available here.
x.No screening until age 30: Pap smears are done every 3 years from age 21.
x.An immediate colposcopy: Colposcopy is done after an abnormal result.

m.A Pap smear with an HPV cotest: applies the 30 and older rule too early

Q.q: A 19-year-old client who is sexually active asks when she needs her first Pap smear. Which response by the nurse is correct?
o: “Your first Pap smear is at age 21.”
“You need one now, because you are sexually active.”
“You should start at age 25 with an HPV test.”
“You should start at age 30 with a cotest.”
“You do not need screening if you receive the HPV vaccine.”
Q.w: No cervical screening is done before age 21. From 21 the Pap is repeated every 3 years. The HPV vaccine at age 11 to 12, and as early as 9, is prevention and does not treat an existing infection. (study guide, Ch 65)

x.\u201cYou need one now, because you are: No screening is done before age 21.
x.\u201cYou should start at age 25 with an: Primary HPV screening may start at 25, but the Pap starts at 21.
x.\u201cYou do not need screening if you r: The vaccine does not replace screening.

Q.q: A nurse reviews screening options for a healthy 40-year-old client. Select all that apply.
o: Primary HPV testing every 5 years
A Pap and HPV cotest every 5 years
A Pap test alone every 3 years
A Pap test alone every year
A Pap test alone every 5 years
Q.w: Cervical cancer develops slowly through dysplasia, and the HPV test finds the virus that causes it earlier than the Pap finds cell changes. Because of that, from age 30 to 65 the interval can be longer when HPV testing is included: primary HPV or a Pap and HPV cotest every 5 years. A Pap alone is repeated every 3 years. Clients with HIV, immunosuppression, DES exposure or prior dysplasia may need screening more often. (study guide, Ch 65)

x.A Pap test alone every year: Pap alone is repeated every 3 years.
x.A Pap test alone every 5 years: Pap alone is every 3 years; the 5-year interval applies to HPV testing.

Q.q: A 67-year-old client has had adequate negative cervical screenings and no history of CIN 2 in the last 20 years. What should the nurse expect about further screening?
o: She may stop screening
She needs a Pap every year for life
She needs a colposcopy every 3 years
She needs a hysterectomy
Q.w: Cervical cancer takes years to develop from dysplasia, so a long record of normal results makes new disease unlikely. After age 65, screening may stop if prior screening was adequate and negative and there has been no CIN 2 in 20 years. A hysterectomy for a benign cause, with no history of CIN 2, also ends screening. Screening continues only when risk is higher. (study guide, Ch 65)

x.She needs a Pap every year for life: Screening may stop after 65 with adequate negative results.
x.She needs a hysterectomy: There is no indication for surgery.

Q.q: A client has an abnormal Pap smear and a positive high-risk HPV test. Which procedure does the nurse expect next?
o: Colposcopy with biopsy
A repeat Pap smear in 3 years
A hysterectomy
A CA-125 blood test
A mammogram
Q.w: An abnormal Pap with high-risk HPV leads to colposcopy: the cervix is swabbed with acetic acid or Lugol's, and abnormal areas are biopsied. The biopsy is diagnostic. MRI, PET, CT and chest x-ray stage the cancer. (study guide, Ch 65 and Ch 64)

x.A repeat Pap smear in 3 years: An abnormal result with high-risk HPV is followed up now.
x.A hysterectomy: Treatment is decided after the biopsy.
x.A CA-125 blood test: CA-125 is an ovarian marker and is not a screening test.

Q.q: A 40-year-old client with invasive cervical cancer reports bleeding after intercourse. Which statement about the clinical manifestations is accurate?
o: Vaginal bleeding, especially after intercourse, is the most common symptom of invasive cancer, while dysplasia has no symptoms
Early dysplasia causes heavy bleeding and pain
Bloating and early satiety are the typical first signs
A hard painless breast lump is typical
Q.w: Cervical dysplasia has no symptoms. Vaginal bleeding, especially postcoital bleeding, is the most common symptom of invasive cancer, and malodorous discharge and pain with intercourse may be present. The nursing focus is prevention through Pap screening and the HPV vaccine. (study guide, Ch 65)

x.Early dysplasia causes heavy bleeding an: Dysplasia has no symptoms and usually cannot be seen.
x.Bloating and early satiety are the typic: That is the pattern of ovarian cancer.

Q.q: A client is scheduled for a colposcopy. Which statement by the client indicates understanding of the preparation?
o: “I will not put anything in my vagina for 24 hours before the test.”
“I need a full bladder for this test.”
“It is fine to use Lugol's solution even though I am allergic to shellfish.”
“I should schedule it for the heaviest day of my period.”
Q.w: Colposcopy magnifies the cervix after an abnormal Pap, and acetic acid or Lugol's solution is applied so abnormal tissue stands out. The client is told to put nothing in the vagina for 24 hours beforehand. The client empties the bladder, and the test is rescheduled during heavy menstruation. Lugol's contains iodine, so it is contraindicated with an iodine or shellfish allergy. (study guide, Ch 64)

x.\u201cI need a full bladder for this tes: The client empties the bladder first; a full bladder is for pelvic ultrasound.
x.\u201cIt is fine to use Lugol's solution: Lugol's is contraindicated with iodine or shellfish allergy.
x.\u201cI should schedule it for the heavi: The test is rescheduled if menstruating heavily.

m.\u201cI need a full bladder for this tes: mixes up colposcopy and ultrasound prep

Q.q: A 29-year-old client with early-stage cervical cancer wants to keep her fertility. Which surgery does the nurse expect to be offered?
o: Radical trachelectomy
Radical hysterectomy with lymph node dissection
Pelvic exenteration
Chemoradiation with brachytherapy
Q.w: Early disease may be treated with cone biopsy or a radical trachelectomy, which removes the cervix only, for a client who wants to keep fertility. Without a fertility wish, simple or radical hysterectomy with node dissection is done. Higher stages use chemoradiation, and pelvic exenteration can cure a pelvic recurrence. (study guide, Ch 65)

x.Radical hysterectomy with lymph node dis: This is for a client who does not desire fertility.
x.Pelvic exenteration: Exenteration is for recurrence confined to the pelvis and removes all pelvic organs.
x.Chemoradiation with brachytherapy: This is used for higher stages and is not a fertility-preserving surgery.

Q.q: A nurse tells a student that most cervical cancers are squamous cell carcinomas that arise in the transformation zone where the endocervix meets the ectocervix. The nurse's statement is accurate.
o: True
False
Q.w: About 90% of cervical cancers are squamous cell carcinomas arising in the transformation zone. Most of the rest are adenocarcinomas of the glandular cells of the endocervix. The Pap samples this junction. (study guide, Ch 65 and Ch 64)

x.False: Marking False denies the main cell type of cervical cancer.

Q.q: A nurse tells a client that HPV vaccination treats an existing HPV infection and makes cervical screening unnecessary. The nurse's statement is accurate.
o: True
False
Q.w: The vaccine is given at age 11 to 12 (it can start at 9) and does not treat an existing infection. Routine screening is still needed. The true version is that vaccination is prevention and screening continues. (study guide, Ch 65)

x.True: Marking True would tell the client to skip screening.

Q.q: A 31-year-old client reports a firm, painless lump in his scrotum with a heavy feeling. Which part of his history is the greatest risk factor for testicular cancer?
o: An undescended testicle in childhood
Klinefelter's syndrome
HIV infection
Cigarette smoking
Down syndrome
Q.w: Cryptorchidism, one or both testes failing to descend from the abdomen into the scrotum, is the greatest risk factor. Others include Down syndrome, Klinefelter's, HIV, family history, cancer in the other testicle and smoking. The average age is 33, and the cure rate is 90 to 100% if it is found early. (study guide, Ch 66)

x.Klinefelter's syndrome: Klinefelter's is a listed risk but not the greatest.
x.HIV infection: HIV is a listed risk but not the greatest.
x.Cigarette smoking: Smoking is listed among others but is not the greatest.
x.Down syndrome: Down syndrome is listed among other risks but is not the greatest.

m.Klinefelter's syndrome: ranks a minor risk above cryptorchidism
m.HIV infection: ranks a minor risk above cryptorchidism
m.Cigarette smoking: ranks a minor risk above cryptorchidism
m.Down syndrome: ranks a minor risk above cryptorchidism

Q.q: A 29-year-old client has a mass in one testicle. Which description of the classic presentation does the nurse expect?
o: A painless mass, sometimes with a firm or heavy feeling in the scrotum
Sudden severe scrotal pain with fever after a kick to the groin
A tender, red, hot scrotum with painful urination
Bright red blood in the semen with urgency
Q.w: The classic sign of testicular cancer is a painless mass. Some men have a dull abdominal ache or a dull scrotal ache, a firm or heavy feeling, swelling and redness. Metastasis may cause GI symptoms, low back pain, gynecomastia, cough or hemoptysis. (study guide, Ch 66)

x.Sudden severe scrotal pain with fever af: Sudden pain after trauma suggests testicular injury, not the classic cancer mass.
x.A tender, red, hot scrotum with painful: Painful, red and hot suggests infection such as epididymitis.
x.Bright red blood in the semen with urgen: That points toward the prostate, not the testis.

Q.q: A client with testicular cancer asks the nurse about the best treatment. Which response is correct?
o: “Treatment for all types starts with removal of the affected testicle.”
“Radiation alone is the best first treatment.”
“Chemotherapy alone is used first for every type.”
“Hormone therapy is the first treatment.”
“Observation with ultrasound is enough for all types.”
Q.w: All types start with orchiectomy through an abdominal incision. Seminoma then gets radiation and/or chemotherapy; nonseminoma gets lymph node removal and chemotherapy, not radiation. Chemotherapy drugs include cisplatin, etoposide, bleomycin, ifosfamide, paclitaxel and vinblastine. (study guide, Ch 66 and class PLQ)

x.\u201cRadiation alone is the best first: Radiation is added after surgery for seminoma only.
x.\u201cHormone therapy is the first treat: Hormone therapy is not the treatment for testicular cancer.
x.\u201cObservation with ultrasound is eno: Removal of the testicle and its blood supply is the starting treatment.

Q.q: A client's AFP and hCG levels stayed elevated after orchiectomy. What does the nurse understand this to mean?
o: More tumor may remain, so further workup is needed
The surgery cured the cancer
The client has developed hypercalcemia
The client has a benign condition
Q.w: Alpha-fetoprotein and hCG are made by testicular tumor cells and enter the blood. Once the tumor is removed the levels should fall. If they stay high, tumor tissue that makes them must still be present somewhere, perhaps in lymph nodes or other organs. The nurse reports persistent elevation, because it means more tumor should be looked for. Staging uses TNM plus S for the serum markers. (study guide, Ch 66)

x.The surgery cured the cancer: These markers should fall after the tumor is removed.
x.The client has developed hypercalcemia: The markers are not calcium results.
x.The client has a benign condition: Persistent elevation points to remaining tumor.

Q.q: The nurse is teaching a client who will start treatment for testicular cancer. Select all that apply.
o: Bank sperm before treatment to preserve fertility
Follow up for at least 10 years
Retroperitoneal lymph node removal can damage nerves that control ejaculation
Report signs of infection after surgery
Fertility is not affected by treatment
Follow-up can stop after 1 year
Chemotherapy has no effect on the kidneys or hearing
Q.w: Bank sperm before treatment, follow up for at least 10 years, and know that retroperitoneal lymph node resection may damage the ejaculation nerves. Report infection signs. Chemotherapy can cause hair loss, mouth sores, nausea, infection, bleeding, kidney damage, neuropathy, ototoxicity, lung damage with bleomycin and hemorrhagic cystitis with ifosfamide. (study guide, Ch 66)

x.Fertility is not affected by treatment: Treatment can affect fertility, which is why sperm banking is offered first.
x.Follow-up can stop after 1 year: Follow-up lasts at least 10 years, the usual window for recurrence.
x.Chemotherapy has no effect on the kidney: Chemotherapy can cause kidney damage and ototoxicity.

Q.q: The nurse reviews testicular cancer facts. Match each item with its description.
o: Slow-growing and very sensitive to radiation
Grows and spreads faster and is not responsive to radiation
Can cause lung damage
Can cause hemorrhagic cystitis
Q.w: Seminoma and nonseminoma behave differently, which decides treatment. Seminoma is slow growing and very sensitive to radiation, so surgery is followed by radiation and/or chemotherapy. Nonseminoma grows and spreads faster and does not respond to radiation, so it gets surgery, node removal and chemotherapy. The chemotherapy drugs also have typical toxicities: bleomycin can injure the lungs and ifosfamide can cause hemorrhagic cystitis. (study guide, Ch 66)

x.Slow-growing and very sensitive to radia: Seminoma occurs in men in their 30s to 40s.
x.Grows and spreads faster and is not resp: Nonseminoma includes embryonal and teratoma types, from teens to 40s.
x.Can cause lung damage: Bleomycin is the chemotherapy listed for lung damage.
x.Can cause hemorrhagic cystitis: Ifosfamide is listed for hemorrhagic cystitis.

Q.q: A client returns from an orchiectomy with a blood pressure of 88/50 mm Hg and a heart rate of 124 beats per minute. What does the nurse suspect?
o: Volume loss
Infection
Pain only
Normal recovery
Q.w: After surgery the body loses blood and fluid from the surgical site, and the heart beats faster to keep the output up. When the volume lost is significant the blood pressure falls, so low blood pressure with a fast heart rate means volume loss. Infection would show as fever instead. The nurse reports the vital signs and watches the wound for bleeding. (study guide, Ch 66)

x.Infection: Fever, not hypotension with tachycardia, points to infection.
x.Pain only: Pain can raise the heart rate but does not lower the blood pressure.

Q.q: A nurse explains to a client that alpha-fetoprotein and hCG levels should fall after the tumor is removed. The nurse's statement is accurate.
o: True
False
Q.w: The tumor cells are the source of AFP and hCG, so when the tumor is removed the markers should drop. A fall confirms that the source was removed. A level that does not fall suggests tumor tissue elsewhere. The nurse therefore follows the markers as a measure of treatment success. (study guide, Ch 66)

x.False: Marking False would make a persistent rise sound normal.

Q.q: A nurse teaches a client with a nonseminoma that radiation is the main treatment because this type is very sensitive to radiation. The nurse's teaching is accurate.
o: True
False
Q.w: Nonseminoma grows and spreads faster and is not responsive to radiation. It is treated with surgery plus lymph node removal, then chemotherapy. Seminoma is the radiation-sensitive type. (study guide, Ch 66)

x.True: Marking True gives nonseminoma the seminoma's radiation sensitivity.

Q.q: A client asks why the provider wants a biopsy when a CT scan already shows a mass. Which response by the nurse is best?
o: “A biopsy is the most specific test and is required for a definite diagnosis of cancer.”
“A CT scan can identify the exact cell type of the tumor.”
“A PET scan is the most specific test for cancer.”
“A tumor marker blood test is enough to confirm cancer.”
“A biopsy is done only after treatment has started.”
Q.w: Labs and imaging are supportive. A biopsy is the most specific way to diagnose cancer and gives tissue for stage and grade. Results take 3 to 10 days. CT shows the mass location, PET shows active areas, and MRI is best for brain, joint and breast. (study guide, Ch 13 and class PLQ)

x.\u201cA CT scan can identify the exact c: CT shows the location and organ or vessel involvement, not the cell type.
x.\u201cA PET scan is the most specific te: A PET scan shows metabolic hot spots and supports the diagnosis.
x.\u201cA tumor marker blood test is enoug: Markers support the diagnosis and track treatment but do not confirm it.
x.\u201cA biopsy is done only after treatm: Tissue is needed to diagnose, stage and grade before treatment.

Q.q: A client with a breast mass is scheduled for an excisional biopsy rather than an incisional biopsy. The client asks why. Which response by the nurse is correct?
o: “An excisional biopsy removes the whole mass with a margin, while an incisional biopsy can track cancer cells through normal tissue.”
“An incisional biopsy removes the whole mass, so it is preferred.”
“An excisional biopsy only suctions a few cells with a needle.”
“An excisional biopsy tests the blood for tumor DNA.”
“Both types carry the same risk of spreading cells.”
Q.w: Excisional biopsy removes the whole mass plus a margin and is preferred. Incisional (core) biopsy cuts into the mass and risks tracking cancer cells through normal tissue. Fine-needle aspiration is less traumatic but yields fewer cells. (study guide, Ch 13)

x.\u201cAn incisional biopsy removes the w: The excisional biopsy removes the whole mass; incisional cuts into the mass.
x.\u201cBoth types carry the same risk of: The incisional type can track cells through normal tissue.

Q.q: The nurse reviews biopsy procedures. Match each with its description.
o: A needle suctions cells from near the skin; less traumatic but fewer cells
A wider needle with a cutter removes a larger sample
An imaging-guided probe with a vacuum and rotating cutter, with no sutures
Finds the first node the cancer drains to and determines the stage
Q.w: FNA, core needle and vacuum-assisted biopsies are different needle methods with different sample sizes. A surgical excision removes a mass under 2.5 cm entirely, and a nonpalpable mass is marked with a hooked wire first. A sentinel node biopsy finds the first node the cancer drains to. (study guide, Ch 13 and Ch 65)

x.A needle suctions cells from near the sk: This is FNA, such as for a breast mass.
x.A wider needle with a cutter removes a l: This is a core needle biopsy.
x.An imaging-guided probe with a vacuum an: This is vacuum-assisted biopsy, done with local anesthesia.
x.Finds the first node the cancer drains t: This is a sentinel node biopsy, using a radioactive tracer or blue dye.

Q.q: A client's sentinel lymph node biopsy is negative for cancer. What does the nurse understand this to mean?
o: No further nodes need to be removed
A full axillary dissection of 20 to 40 nodes is still required
The cancer has metastasized to bone
The tumor is stage IV
Q.w: The sentinel node is the first node the cancer would reach, found with a radioactive tracer or blue dye, and it determines the stage. If it is negative, the full axillary dissection can be skipped. If it is positive, an axillary dissection of 20 to 40 nodes follows. (study guide, Ch 65)

x.A full axillary dissection of 20 to 40 n: Axillary dissection is done when the sentinel node is positive.
x.The cancer has metastasized to bone: The sentinel node does not show bone spread.
x.The tumor is stage IV: A negative sentinel node does not make a stage IV tumor.

Q.q: A client has a pelvic mass thought to be ovarian cancer. The client asks why the provider is not doing a needle biopsy of the mass. Which response is correct?
o: “A biopsy could spread the cancer cells; the diagnosis is made by removing the mass surgically and examining it.”
“A needle biopsy is always done first for ovarian masses.”
“A CA-125 blood test is enough to diagnose ovarian cancer.”
“A Pap smear will confirm the diagnosis.”
Q.w: A biopsy of an ovarian mass is not recommended because it could spread the cancer. The definitive diagnosis is surgical removal of the mass plus pathology. In uterine cancer the endometrial biopsy is 99% sensitive for high-grade cancer, and D&C is done if the biopsy is negative but bleeding continues. (study guide, Ch 65)

x.\u201cA needle biopsy is always done fir: Biopsy of an ovarian mass is not recommended.
x.\u201cA CA-125 blood test is enough to d: CA-125 is normal in 50% of early cases and also rises with other conditions.

m.\u201cA needle biopsy is always done fir: applies breast biopsy habits to the ovary

Q.q: A client is scheduled for a bone marrow aspiration and biopsy. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?
o: “Odds are I will die from this procedure.”
“I will feel pressure when the needle goes in.”
“I may feel a brief pulling pain when the marrow is drawn out.”
“I will keep the dressing on for at least 24 hours.”
Q.w: The procedure takes 5 to 10 minutes and a mild sedative is allowed. The client feels pressure on insertion and a brief pulling pain on aspiration, and may hear crunching. A statement that the client will die from it shows fear and misinformation and needs correction. (study guide, Ch 33 and class PLQ)

Q.q: The nurse prepares a client for a bone marrow biopsy at the most common site. Which position does the nurse use?
o: Prone or side-lying, for the posterior iliac crest
Supine, because the most common site is the sternum
Sitting upright with the arms crossed
Trendelenburg
Q.w: The most common site is the posterior iliac crest, with the client prone or side-lying. The sternum or anterior iliac crest is done supine. Before the procedure: consent, allergies and bleeding risk (platelets, coagulation studies, anticoagulants). (study guide, Ch 33)

x.Supine, because the most common site is: The most common site is the posterior iliac crest; the sternum and anterior iliac crest use supine.
x.Sitting upright with the arms crossed: This does not expose the posterior iliac crest.
x.Trendelenburg: This position is not used for this procedure.

m.Supine, because the most common site is: swaps the common site and position

Q.q: The nurse provides care after a bone marrow biopsy. Select all that apply.
o: Hold direct pressure for 5 to 10 minutes and apply a sterile dressing
Have the client rest for several hours
Leave the dressing on for at least 24 hours
Report bleeding that soaks the dressing or lasts more than 24 hours
Remove the dressing after 1 hour to inspect the site
Encourage vigorous exercise right away
Q.w: After the procedure the nurse applies direct pressure for 5 to 10 minutes and a sterile dressing, and the client rests for several hours. The dressing stays on at least 24 hours. Bleeding that soaks the dressing or lasts more than 24 hours is reported, and the nurse watches for infection and gives analgesia. (study guide, Ch 33)

x.Remove the dressing after 1 hour to insp: The dressing stays on at least 24 hours.
x.Encourage vigorous exercise right away: The client rests for several hours.

Q.q: A client asks what a liquid biopsy is. Which description by the nurse is accurate?
o: A blood test that looks for cancer cells or tumor DNA
Removal of the whole mass with a margin
A needle that suctions cells from a mass
A scope that looks inside the airways
Q.w: A liquid biopsy is a blood test that looks for cancer cells or tumor DNA, so it does not take tissue from the mass. It is used for example in non-small cell lung, breast, colorectal, GI and ovarian cancers. It differs from tissue biopsies, which remove cells or a mass directly. (study guide, Ch 13)

Q.q: A nurse tells a client that the results of a tissue biopsy usually take 3 to 10 days. The nurse's statement is accurate.
o: True
False
Q.w: A biopsy sample has to be processed, stained and examined by a pathologist before a cytopathologic diagnosis can be made, and that takes time. Results are expected in 3 to 10 days. The nurse explains the purpose, preparation, aftercare and when results arrive, so the client is not left waiting without information. The statement is accurate. (study guide, Ch 13)

x.False: Marking False gives the client an unrealistic expectation about when results arrive.

Q.q: A nurse tells a client that blood tests and imaging can give a definitive diagnosis of cancer without a biopsy. The nurse's statement is accurate.
o: True
False
Q.w: Labs and imaging are supportive. A biopsy is required for a definitive cytopathologic diagnosis. The true version is that tissue confirmation is needed. (study guide, Ch 13)

x.True: Marking True treats supportive tests as diagnostic.

Q.q: A 60-year-old postmenopausal client calls the clinic. Which statement requires the nurse's immediate follow-up?
o: “I have had some vaginal bleeding.”
“I feel a little tired in the afternoons.”
“I have mild joint stiffness in the mornings.”
“I had trouble falling asleep last night.”
“I had heartburn after a spicy dinner.”
Q.w: After menopause the uterine lining should not bleed, so bleeding means the lining is abnormal. Uterine cancer is most common at ages 55 to 65, with a median of 60, and abnormal bleeding is its most common symptom. Any postmenopausal bleeding needs evaluation, so this statement is the one that needs immediate follow-up. The other statements are not the key warning sign for a gynecologic cancer. (study guide, Ch 65 and class PLQ)

x.\u201cI feel a little tired in the after: Mild afternoon fatigue is not the red flag for uterine cancer.
x.\u201cI have mild joint stiffness in the: This is not the key warning sign for a gynecologic cancer.
x.\u201cI had trouble falling asleep last: This is not the key warning sign for a gynecologic cancer.
x.\u201cI had heartburn after a spicy dinn: This is not the key warning sign for a gynecologic cancer.

Q.q: The nurse reviews risk factors for uterine (endometrial) cancer. Select all that apply.
o: Unopposed estrogen exposure
Obesity
Tamoxifen use
Early menarche and late menopause
Polycystic ovary syndrome
Estrogen given together with progesterone
Maintaining a healthy weight and exercising
HPV infection
Q.w: Estrogen makes the uterine lining grow, and progesterone balances it. When estrogen is unopposed, by estrogen therapy without progesterone, tamoxifen or anovulation, the lining keeps growing and can become cancer. Obesity adds risk because fat tissue makes estrogen. Chapter 13 also lists early menarche, late menopause, PCOS and diabetes. (study guide, Ch 65 and Ch 13)

x.Estrogen given together with progesteron: Progesterone with estrogen is protective; the risk is estrogen without progesterone.
x.HPV infection: HPV is the cause of cervical cancer.

Q.q: A nurse is describing the most common type of uterine cancer to a client. Which description is correct?
o: Endometrioid adenocarcinoma, which is estrogen-driven and usually found early
Serous or clear cell carcinoma, which is the most common type
Uterine sarcoma, which is the most common type
Squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix
Q.w: Most uterine cancers arise from the lining, the endometrium. About 80% are endometrioid adenocarcinoma, called type I, which is driven by estrogen and is usually found early with about 88% survival. Type II (serous or clear cell) is aggressive and occurs in older clients with a poor prognosis, and sarcoma of the muscle is only 3 to 5%. The most common type is therefore the estrogen-driven endometrioid type. (study guide, Ch 65)

x.Serous or clear cell carcinoma, which is: Type II serous or clear cell cancers are aggressive and occur in older clients, but they are not the most common.
x.Squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix: That is the main type of cervical cancer.

Q.q: A postmenopausal client has vaginal bleeding. Which diagnostic test does the nurse expect to be done first for uterine cancer?
o: Endometrial biopsy
CA-125 blood test
Colposcopy
Mammogram
Q.w: Bleeding comes from the endometrium, so the test samples the endometrium. The endometrial biopsy is 99% sensitive for high-grade cancer and is done first. A pelvic transvaginal ultrasound shows a thickened endometrium, and a D&C is added if the biopsy is negative but bleeding continues. CA-125, colposcopy and mammography belong to ovarian, cervical and breast evaluation. (study guide, Ch 65)

x.Colposcopy: Colposcopy is for the cervix after an abnormal Pap.

Q.q: A client's endometrial biopsy is negative but she continues to have postmenopausal bleeding. Which procedure does the nurse expect?
o: Dilation and curettage
No further testing is needed
Repeat screening in 3 years
A bone marrow biopsy
Q.w: A biopsy takes a small sample and can miss an area of disease, so a negative result does not explain ongoing bleeding. A D&C scrapes the whole lining and gives a larger tissue sample for pathology. It is done with NPO status and consent, and normal postoperative bleeding and cramping are expected. Continued bleeding always needs further evaluation. (study guide, Ch 65 and Ch 64)

x.A bone marrow biopsy: This is for blood and marrow disorders.

Q.q: A client has stage I uterine cancer. Which treatment does the nurse expect?
o: Surgery to remove the uterus, fallopian tubes and ovaries
Chemotherapy alone
Observation only
Pelvic exenteration
Radical trachelectomy
Q.w: Surgery removes the uterus, tubes and ovaries plus washings and lymphadenectomy, and early stage I is often cured by surgery alone. Progestin therapy is used for stage I if surgery is not possible. Radiation is the usual adjuvant. (study guide, Ch 65)

x.Chemotherapy alone: Chemotherapy is for higher-risk disease and gives only a modest response.
x.Observation only: Early stage I is often cured by surgery.
x.Pelvic exenteration: Exenteration is for a pelvic recurrence of cervical cancer.
x.Radical trachelectomy: This surgery is for early cervical cancer.

Q.q: A 52-year-old client with a uterus is prescribed estrogen for menopausal symptoms. Which statement should the nurse include in teaching to lower the risk of uterine cancer?
o: “Estrogen is taken with progesterone because estrogen alone can cause the lining of the uterus to overgrow.”
“Estrogen is safe alone because it protects the uterus.”
“Estrogen should be stopped if you gain weight.”
“Only women who have had a hysterectomy need progesterone.”
Q.w: Anyone on estrogen who has a uterus needs progesterone too. Tamoxifen users need monitoring for endometrial hyperplasia. Prevention also includes a healthy weight and exercise. (study guide, Ch 65)

x.\u201cEstrogen is safe alone because it: Estrogen alone is unopposed and raises uterine cancer risk.
x.\u201cEstrogen should be stopped if you: Weight management helps, but the key point is progesterone.
x.\u201cOnly women who have had a hysterec: The women who need it are those with a uterus.

m.\u201cEstrogen is safe alone because it: forgets that estrogen alone is a risk

Q.q: A client receiving chemotherapy for uterine cancer has stomatitis. Which instruction by the nurse is correct?
o: Avoid hot or spicy food and use salt-water rinses
Eat hot soups to soothe the mouth
Use a hard toothbrush to keep the mouth clean
Avoid fluids to keep the mouth dry
Q.w: Chemotherapy kills fast-dividing cells, including the lining of the mouth, so sores develop. Hot or spicy food irritates the damaged lining and worsens pain. Salt-water rinses keep the mouth clean and comfortable, and antiemetics help with nausea. Soft toothbrushes and good hydration also help. (study guide, Ch 65 and Ch 13)

x.Avoid fluids to keep the mouth dry: Fluids help; dryness worsens mouth sores.

Q.q: A nurse teaches a client that anyone who takes estrogen therapy and has a uterus also needs progesterone. The nurse's teaching is accurate.
o: True
False
Q.w: Estrogen makes the lining of the uterus grow, and progesterone keeps that growth in check. Estrogen alone is unopposed, and years of unopposed growth raise the risk of uterine cancer. A client who has a uterus therefore takes progesterone with estrogen. The teaching is accurate. (study guide, Ch 65)

x.False: Marking False would leave estrogen unopposed.

Q.q: A nurse tells a client that ovarian cancer is the most common gynecologic cancer in the United States. The nurse's statement is accurate.
o: True
False
Q.w: Two different facts are easy to swap. Uterine (endometrial) cancer is the most common gynecologic cancer in the US, with a 2.6% lifetime risk. Ovarian cancer is the deadliest, because its symptoms are vague and 70 to 75% are not found until stage III or IV. The statement gives the label of the wrong cancer and is false. (study guide, Ch 65)

x.True: Marking True swaps the most common gynecologic cancer with the deadliest one.

Q.q: A client receiving chemotherapy has an absolute neutrophil count of 480/mm³. Which nursing action is the priority?
o: Implement neutropenic precautions, including a private room and hand hygiene by everyone
Implement bleeding precautions
Encourage visitors and fresh flowers to lift the client's mood
Take the client's temperature rectally
Offer iron-rich foods
Q.w: Neutropenia is an ANC below 1,500, and neutropenic precautions start at 500 or below. A fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher means broad-spectrum IV antibiotics immediately. The nurse uses hand hygiene, a private room and restricts visitors with communicable diseases. (study guide, Ch 13 and Ch 34)

x.Implement bleeding precautions: Bleeding precautions are for a low platelet count.
x.Encourage visitors and fresh flowers to: Crowds and live plants are avoided in neutropenia.
x.Take the client's temperature rectally: Rectal temperatures are never used in neutropenia.
x.Offer iron-rich foods: Iron foods are for iron deficiency anemia.

Q.q: The nurse is teaching a client with neutropenia about precautions at home. Select all that apply.
o: Wash hands often and ask visitors to do the same
Avoid crowds and people who are sick
Avoid live plants and cut flowers
Avoid standing water, such as in a humidifier
Keep fresh cut flowers in the bedroom
Take the temperature rectally when ill
Eat raspberries and blackberries as a healthy snack
Q.w: Neutrophils are the first cells to reach an infection, so with a low count even ordinary germs can cause serious infection. Each precaution removes a source of germs: other people's hands and coughs, live plants and flowers that carry bacteria and mold, standing water, fruit that is hard to wash, and the rectal route. The client washes produce, avoids raspberries and blackberries, and uses no rectal temperatures, suppositories or enemas. Your class notes add reverse isolation, where staff wear PPE to protect the client. (study guide, Ch 34 Box 34.2 and class notes)

x.Keep fresh cut flowers in the bedroom: Live plants and cut flowers carry bacteria and mold.
x.Take the temperature rectally when ill: No rectal temperatures, suppositories or enemas; rectal bacteria can enter the blood.
x.Eat raspberries and blackberries as a he: Raspberries and blackberries are bumpy and hard to wash, so they are avoided.

m.Keep fresh cut flowers in the bedroom: forgets that plants and flowers carry mold

Q.q: A client with neutropenia is being discharged. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?
o: “I will put fresh cut flowers on my bedside table to cheer me up.”
“I will wash raw fruits and vegetables well.”
“I will check my temperature every day and call if it is above 100.4°F.”
“I will take my antibiotics every day and finish the whole course.”
Q.w: Live plants and cut flowers carry bacteria and mold, and a neutropenic client cannot fight them off. For that reason they are avoided at home and in the hospital, and a statement about placing flowers at the bedside shows a need for teaching. The correct statements are washing raw fruits and vegetables, checking the temperature daily and calling for more than 100.4°F (38°C), and taking prophylactic antimicrobials daily and finishing the course. These actions lower the chance of infection or catch it early. (study guide, Ch 34 Box 34.2)

x.\u201cI will take my antibiotics every d: This is correct teaching; prophylactic antimicrobials are taken daily.

Q.q: A client at home who is receiving chemotherapy has a temperature of 100.6°F (38.1°C). Which instruction by the nurse is correct?
o: “Seek care or call your provider right away, because IV antibiotics can prevent sepsis.”
“Take acetaminophen and call tomorrow if it persists.”
“Drink extra fluids and recheck in 12 hours.”
“A low-grade fever is expected and can be ignored.”
Q.w: In a chemotherapy client, few working neutrophils means the usual signs of infection may be weak or missing, and a fever may be the only sign. An infection can spread to the blood and lead to sepsis within hours. Treatment with IV antibiotics prevents that, so the client should seek care or call the provider right away. Waiting to see whether the fever settles delays treatment. (study guide, Ch 13 and Ch 34)

x.\u201cTake acetaminophen and call tomorr: Waiting delays treatment; fever may be the only sign of infection.
x.\u201cA low-grade fever is expected and: A temperature of 100.4°F or higher requires immediate care.

Q.q: The nurse reviews the orders of a client with an ANC of 450/mm³. Which order should the nurse question?
o: Bisacodyl rectal suppository as needed for constipation
Prophylactic levofloxacin daily
Oral temperature every 4 hours
Private room with strict hand hygiene
Q.w: Rectal tissue is full of bacteria, and a suppository, enema or thermometer can create tiny tears that let them into the blood. With an ANC of 450 the client cannot control that infection. For that reason rectal medications and temperatures are not used in neutropenia. Prophylactic antibiotics, a private room and oral temperatures are appropriate. (study guide, Ch 34 Box 34.2)

x.Prophylactic levofloxacin daily: Prophylactic antibiotics are used in neutropenia.
x.Private room with strict hand hygiene: This is part of neutropenic precautions.

Q.q: A client with leukemia is neutropenic. Which visitor should the nurse restrict?
o: A sibling who has a cold and a cough
A well adult friend who has washed her hands
The client's spouse who is well and wears a mask as requested
An asymptomatic adult relative who sanitizes his hands
Q.w: A neutropenic client has few cells to fight germs, so any visitor with a communicable illness is a direct risk. A sibling with a cold and a cough could pass on the infection. Well visitors who clean their hands are allowed. The plan also avoids crowds, small children and pets, and requires hand hygiene by everyone. (study guide, Ch 34 and class PLQ)

x.A well adult friend who has washed her h: A healthy visitor using hand hygiene is allowed.
x.An asymptomatic adult relative who sanit: A well adult with hand hygiene is allowed.

Q.q: The nurse reviews neutropenia values with a new graduate. Match each value with its meaning.
o: Neutropenia and an infection risk
Neutropenic precautions begin
Call the provider immediately
Q.w: The ANC counts the neutrophils that can fight bacteria and fungi. Below 1,500 the client is neutropenic and at risk of infection, and at 500 or below the risk is high enough that neutropenic precautions are started. A temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher in a chemotherapy client is called in immediately and treated with broad-spectrum IV antibiotics. Matching each number with its action is the core of the care plan. (study guide, Ch 13 and Ch 34)

x.Neutropenic precautions begin: At an ANC of 500 or below the client is on neutropenic precautions, and IV antibiotics are given for fever.
x.Call the provider immediately: A fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher in a chemotherapy client is called in right away.

Q.q: A nurse explains that in reverse isolation for a neutropenic client the nurse wears protective equipment to protect the client from infection. The nurse's explanation is accurate.
o: True
False
Q.w: In ordinary isolation the barrier protects other people from the client's germs. In reverse isolation the direction is reversed, because the neutropenic client is the one who cannot fight germs. Staff and visitors wear PPE when required, limit their exposures, and avoid items that harbor waterborne organisms. The nurse explaining that the PPE protects the client is accurate. (class notes and study guide, Ch 34)

x.False: Marking False would turn it into isolation that protects others instead.

Q.q: A nurse tells a neutropenic client that raspberries and blackberries are safe to eat because they are easy to wash. The nurse's statement is accurate.
o: True
False
Q.w: Fruits and vegetables carry soil bacteria on their surface, and a neutropenic client cannot fight them off. Raspberries and blackberries have a bumpy surface that traps dirt and is hard to clean. For that reason they are avoided, while other raw fruits and vegetables are washed well. The statement is false. (study guide, Ch 34 Box 34.2)

x.True: Marking True would let the client eat fruit that is hard to clean.

c-risk-list.title: The risk factor categories
points: The nine risk factor categories are carcinogens, environment, hormones, genetics, lifestyle, infectious disease, medications, immune status and nutrition.
Carcinogen exposure is the most common risk factor, and risks are cumulative.
Age and genetics cannot be changed; 5 to 10% of cancers come from known genetic syndromes such as BRCA1/2.

Hereditary red flags are multiple primaries, bilateral tumors in paired organs, a younger-than-usual age, a tumor in the sex not usually affected, and two or more first-degree relatives with the same cancer.
BRCA2 also raises the risk of pancreatic and prostate cancer and melanoma.

c-risk-table.title: Risk factors by cancer (Table 13.2)
points: Cervical cancer: HPV, multiple partners, early sexual contact, tobacco use.
Gastric cancer: H. pylori, alcohol, ulcers, smoking. Liver cancer: alcohol and hepatitis A, B or C.
Testicular cancer: undescended testicle is the greatest risk. Lung cancer: tobacco, asbestos, coal, soot, tar, pollution, wood dust.
Uterine cancer: estrogen therapy without progesterone, obesity, tamoxifen, PCOS, diabetes.

c-risk-prev.title: Levels of prevention
points: Primary prevention: risk factor modification, immunization (HPV, hepatitis), chemoprevention and avoiding carcinogens.
Secondary prevention: screening for early detection (breast, cervical, colon, prostate).
Tertiary prevention: reducing morbidity and mortality once disease is diagnosed.
c-risk-prev.source: study guide, Ch 13 and class notes

c-risk-caution.title: CAUTION warning signs
points: C change in bowel or bladder habits; A a sore that does not heal; U unusual bleeding or discharge; T thickening or lump.
I indigestion or difficulty swallowing; O obvious change in a wart or mole; N nagging cough or hoarseness.
A sign lasting more than 2 weeks needs evaluation.

c-stage-tnm.title: TNM, stages and grade
points: T is the size of the tumor, N is the number of lymph nodes involved, and M is the presence of metastasis; M1 means the cancer is not local.
Stage I is small with no obvious spread outside the organ, stage II invades deeper tissue or local nodes, stage III is large or locally advanced, and stage IV has metastasized.
All hematologic malignancies are stage IV at diagnosis.
Grade describes how differentiated the cells are; poorly differentiated cells are more aggressive.
c-stage-tnm.source: study guide, Ch 13 and class PLQ

c-stage-sizes.title: Size and stage tables
points: Breast sizes: 2 cm or less is stage I, 2 to 5 cm is stage II, over 5 cm is stage IIB or III; nodes 4 to 8 is IIIA, up to 9 is IIIB, 10 or more is IIIC.
Prostate: T1 cannot be felt, T2 is confined to the prostate, T3 is locally extensive, T4 invades neighboring organs.
Gleason is two grades of 1 to 5 added together, maximum 10; higher is worse.
Ovarian FIGO: I ovaries, II pelvis, III peritoneum and/or nodes, IV distant.

c-bx-types.title: Biopsy types and what they prove
points: A biopsy is the most specific test and is required for a definite diagnosis; labs and imaging are supportive; results take 3 to 10 days.
Excisional biopsy removes the whole mass with a margin and is preferred; incisional (core) biopsy can track cells through normal tissue.
Fine-needle aspiration is less traumatic but gives fewer cells; core needle gives a larger sample; vacuum-assisted uses a probe with no sutures.
A negative sentinel node means no further nodes are removed; a positive one leads to an axillary dissection of 20 to 40 nodes.
A liquid biopsy is a blood test for cancer cells or tumor DNA.

c-bx-site.title: Biopsy by site
points: Ovarian mass: biopsy is not recommended because it could spread cells; the diagnosis is surgical removal with pathology.
Uterine: endometrial biopsy is 99% sensitive for high-grade cancer; a D&C is done if the biopsy is negative but bleeding continues.
Cervical: colposcopy with biopsy after an abnormal Pap; the biopsy is diagnostic.
Lung: bronchoscopy views and biopsies the airways; mediastinoscopy is an incision to biopsy the mediastinum.
c-bx-site.source: study guide, Ch 13, Ch 26 and Ch 65

c-bx-marrow.title: Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy
points: The most common site is the posterior iliac crest with the client prone or side-lying; the sternum or anterior iliac crest is done supine.
Before: consent, allergies and bleeding risk. The client feels pressure and a brief pulling pain, and the procedure takes 5 to 10 minutes.
After: direct pressure for 5 to 10 minutes, a sterile dressing, rest for several hours, dressing on at least 24 hours.
Report bleeding that soaks the dressing or lasts more than 24 hours, and watch for infection.

c-lung-types.title: Small cell versus non-small cell
points: Small cell is about 15%, grows fast and spreads early, has a poor outlook (class: 6 months to 1 year), and surgery is not the main treatment.
Non-small cell is about 85%, has three types (adenocarcinoma, squamous cell, large cell), is slower, and has a good 5-year survival if found early.
More than 90% of lung cancer is caused by smoking; yearly low-dose CT is for high-risk clients (20 pack-years, current smoker or quit within 15 years).
c-lung-types.source: study guide, Ch 26 and class notes

c-lung-dx.title: Lung cancer cues and diagnosis
points: Cues: new or changed cough, hemoptysis, shortness of breath, wheezing, hoarseness, chest pain, weight loss, frequent pneumonia.
Headache and bone pain suggest metastasis to brain and bone; common sites are brain, bone, adrenal gland and the other lung.
PET shows metabolic activity, not structure; sputum cytology, bronchoscopy and mediastinoscopy obtain cells or tissue.

c-lung-tx.title: Lung cancer treatment
points: Lobectomy removes a lobe, pneumonectomy removes a lung, and a wedge resection removes a small section; surgery is preferred if there is no metastasis.
Chemotherapy is the primary treatment for advanced disease; radiation is used when surgery is not an option or for palliation.
WHO ladder: nonopioid, then moderate opioid plus nonopioid, then strong opioid plus nonopioid, given around the clock.
Palliative care begins at diagnosis.

c-lung-nursing.title: Lung cancer nursing care and chest tubes
points: Give oxygen to keep the SpO₂ at 90% or higher and position the client in semi-Fowler's.
Small frequent meals with supplements; a large meal pushes on the diaphragm.
Never clamp a chest tube; keep the system closed; continuous bubbling in the water-seal chamber is an air leak.

c-labs-cbc.title: CBC, WBC and ANC
points: A CBC uses a lavender (EDTA) tube; PT, INR and PTT use sodium citrate.
A left shift is many immature neutrophils (bands) and means active infection.
Neutropenia is an ANC below 1,500; 500 or below needs neutropenic precautions.
Reticulocytes are immature RBCs: high means the marrow is responding, low means a hypoproliferative marrow.
Low MCV is microcytic (iron deficiency); high MCV is macrocytic (B12 or folate).

c-labs-plt.title: Platelet thresholds
points: Normal platelets are 150,000 to 450,000/mm³.
Bleeding precautions start below 100,000; spontaneous bleeding is possible below 50,000.
Platelets are usually transfused below 20,000; below 5,000 a fatal CNS or GI bleed is possible.

c-labs-iron.title: Iron studies and the iron diet
points: In iron deficiency ferritin and transferrin saturation are low, TIBC is high, and the cells are microcytic and hypochromic.
No iron supplements for 24 hours before a serum iron; draw it in the morning.
Eat heme iron (red meat) and nonheme iron (spinach, beans) with vitamin C; dairy blocks absorption.

c-labs-coag.title: Clotting studies
points: The intrinsic pathway is monitored by PTT and heparin; the extrinsic pathway by PT/INR and warfarin.
The INR goal on warfarin is 2 to 3.
Bleeding time checks platelet function and is not done if platelets are under 75,000; platelet aggregation is impaired by aspirin, NSAIDs and von Willebrand disease.

c-leuk-patho.title: What leukemia does
points: A stem cell mutates into immature blasts that never mature or die, producing leukocytosis.
The crowded marrow cannot make enough RBCs and platelets, so anemia and thrombocytopenia occur.
The blasts cannot fight infection, so neutropenia and infection occur.
AML and ALL are acute and ALL is the most common childhood leukemia; CML and CLL are chronic and can turn acute.

c-leuk-risk.title: Leukemia risk factors
points: Risk factors are genetic anomalies, Down syndrome, radiation, benzene or chemical exposure, prior chemotherapy or radiation, and smoking.
The Philadelphia chromosome (9;22) is found in more than 90% of CML.
Oil refinery work means benzene exposure, the highest risk factor in the case.

c-leuk-tx.title: Leukemia treatment and medications
points: Chemotherapy is given in phases: induction (get remission), consolidation (treat hidden disease), maintenance (prevent relapse); remission is not a cure.
AML induction example is daunorubicin plus cytarabine; imatinib targets Bcr-Abl in CML; ibrutinib is used in CLL.
Prophylactic antibiotics, antivirals and antifungals are given during neutropenia.
Radiation to the brain and spine treats CNS disease because chemotherapy cannot cross the blood–brain barrier.
The textbook says G-CSF (filgrastim) is generally not indicated in leukemia.

c-leuk-nursing.title: Leukemia nursing priorities
points: After chemotherapy the first priority is infection; fever means broad-spectrum IV antibiotics immediately.
Never take a rectal temperature in a neutropenic client.
Teach to avoid dental cleanings when platelets are low, and go to the ED for fever of 102°F, chills or a nosebleed over 10 minutes.
Offer sperm or egg banking before therapy.

c-neut-def.title: Neutropenia values and fever
points: Neutropenia is an ANC below 1,500; precautions start at 500 or below.
A temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher needs immediate care and IV antibiotics.
Fever may be the first and only sign of infection.

c-neut-prec.title: Neutropenic precautions (Box 34.2)
points: Hand hygiene by everyone, a private room, avoid crowds, sick people, small children and pets.
No live plants or cut flowers, no standing water or humidifiers.
Wash raw fruits and vegetables well; avoid raspberries and blackberries.
No rectal temperatures, suppositories or enemas, because rectal bacteria can enter the blood.
Take prophylactic antimicrobials daily and finish the course; reverse isolation means staff wear PPE to protect the client.
c-neut-prec.source: study guide, Ch 34 and class notes

c-hodg-dx.title: Hodgkin lymphoma: signs and diagnosis
points: Reed–Sternberg cells define Hodgkin lymphoma; it has a better survival rate than non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
Painless lymph node swelling; B symptoms are low-grade fever, drenching night sweats and weight loss.
Itching is common in Hodgkin lymphoma; a dry cough worse lying flat suggests a mediastinal mass.
A lymph node biopsy is definitive; uric acid and LDH are elevated.

c-hodg-comp.title: Lymphoma complications and nursing
points: Superior vena cava syndrome: facial and arm swelling, dyspnea, chest pain, dysphagia.
Spinal cord compression: back pain, then sensory and motor change; an emergency.
Hypercalcemia above 11 mg/dL: confusion, polyuria, heart block; IV fluids dilute calcium.
Lymphoma staging: I one node, II two or more nodes on one side of the diaphragm, III both sides, IV organs plus nodes.
Teach neutropenic and bleeding precautions before chemotherapy.

c-mm-patho.title: Myeloma: patho and CRAB
points: A clone of plasma cells makes an M protein; lytic bone lesions release calcium.
CRAB: hypercalcemia above 11.5, renal insufficiency (creatinine above 2), anemia (Hgb below 10), bone disease.
Excess light chains (Bence Jones protein) are toxic to the kidneys.
Myeloma is an incurable B-cell cancer of plasma cells.

c-mm-nursing.title: Myeloma nursing interventions
points: Encourage fluids to dilute calcium and protect the kidneys; monitor serum and urine calcium, BUN and creatinine.
Encourage ambulation as tolerated and position for comfort.
Bisphosphonates such as ibandronate (Boniva) reduce bone breakdown, which lowers calcium and fractures.
Sudden severe pain or new numbness may mean a fracture or cord compression: report at once.
Thalidomide and lenalidomide are teratogenic.
c-mm-nursing.source: study guide, Ch 34 and class notes

c-breast-tx.title: Breast cancer treatment
points: Lumpectomy is always followed by radiation; with chemotherapy the order is surgery, chemotherapy, then radiation.
Neoadjuvant therapy is given before the primary treatment; adjuvant therapy is given after.
DCIS is stage 0 and requires surgery; LCIS has no treatment and is followed with mammograms.

c-breast-meds.title: Breast cancer medications (Table 65.3)
points: Tamoxifen blocks estrogen at its receptor for 5 to 10 years; avoid SSRIs and question oral contraceptives in estrogen-positive disease.
Aromatase inhibitors (anastrozole, letrozole, exemestane) stop androgens becoming estrogen; they risk osteoporosis and fractures.
Trastuzumab is for HER2-positive tumors and can cause cardiotoxicity; pembrolizumab is immunotherapy with rash, diarrhea and thyroid problems.
c-breast-meds.source: study guide, Ch 65 and Davis Table 65.3

c-breast-male.title: Male breast cancer
points: It is about 100 times less common than in women, occurs at ages 60 to 70, and BRCA2 is the more common mutation.
With little breast tissue it spreads early to the nipple, skin and muscle; mastectomy is usual.
Hormone therapy is only for receptor-positive tumors, so question antiestrogen therapy in a receptor-negative client.
Ultrasound is used under age 25; mammogram at 25 or older.

c-breast-nursing.title: Breast cancer nursing care
points: Bloody drainage saturating the dressing is the most concerning wound finding; serosanguineous drainage is expected.
Lymphedema follows axillary node removal; shoulder immobility is the most common long-term effect.
Radiation effects: skin redness, itching, desquamation, breast swelling, and pneumonitis 6 weeks to 6 months later.
Breast self-exam is not recommended; screening is by mammography.

c-ut-risk.title: Uterine cancer risk
points: The most common gynecologic cancer in the US, usually at ages 55 to 65.
The number one risk factors are unopposed estrogen and obesity; tamoxifen, early menarche, late menopause, PCOS and diabetes add risk.
About 80% are endometrioid adenocarcinoma; anyone on estrogen with a uterus needs progesterone.

c-ut-dx.title: Uterine cancer diagnosis and treatment
points: Abnormal uterine or postmenopausal bleeding is the most common symptom and needs evaluation.
Endometrial biopsy first; ultrasound shows a thickened endometrium; D&C if the biopsy is negative but bleeding continues.
Treatment is removal of the uterus, tubes and ovaries; radiation is the usual adjuvant.
Stomatitis: salt-water rinses and avoid hot or spicy food.

c-cerv-screen.title: Cervical screening guidelines
points: No screening before age 21; the first Pap is at 21 and is repeated every 3 years until 29.
HPV testing is not a screen at 21 to 29, except as a reflex if atypical cells are found; primary HPV may start at 25 every 5 years.
Ages 30 to 65: primary HPV or Pap plus HPV cotest every 5 years, or Pap alone every 3 years.
Screening may stop after 65 with adequate negative results and no CIN 2 in 20 years.
c-cerv-screen.source: study guide, Ch 65 and class PLQ

c-cerv-dx.title: Cervical cancer cause, signs and work-up
points: HPV is the cause; the HPV vaccine at age 11 to 12 (as early as 9) does not treat an existing infection.
Dysplasia has no symptoms; vaginal bleeding, especially after intercourse, is the most common symptom of invasive cancer.
An abnormal Pap with high-risk HPV leads to colposcopy with biopsy; nothing in the vagina for 24 hours before, and Lugol's is contraindicated with iodine or shellfish allergy.
About 90% are squamous cell carcinomas in the transformation zone.

c-cerv-tx.title: Cervical cancer treatment
points: Early disease: cone biopsy or radical trachelectomy if fertility is wanted; hysterectomy with node dissection if not.
Higher stages: chemoradiation with brachytherapy.
Pelvic exenteration can cure a recurrence confined to the pelvis.

c-pros-patho.title: Prostate cancer patho and screening
points: Tumors grow on the periphery of the gland, so urinary symptoms come late; spread is to lymph nodes, bone, rectum and bladder.
PSA of 4 ng/mL or higher needs further assessment; PSA has high sensitivity but low specificity and cannot tell BPH from cancer.
A needle biopsy confirms the diagnosis, followed by a Gleason score.
African American men have a higher incidence and twice the mortality; BPH is not a precursor to prostate cancer.

c-pros-tx.title: Prostate cancer treatment and safety
points: Brachytherapy seeds are placed permanently through the perineum for cancer confined to the prostate; no sex for 2 weeks, then use a condom.
The nurse minimizes contact and wears proper, thicker PPE with brachytherapy; an external beam client is not radioactive.
Ablative hormone therapy suppresses testosterone; chemotherapy is for hormone-refractory disease.
c-pros-tx.source: study guide, Ch 66 and class notes

c-pros-postop.title: Post-op complications after prostatectomy
points: Impotence is the most expected; nerve-sparing surgery only tries to protect the erection nerves.
Watch for urinary incontinence, infection (fever, pain, swelling, redness) and bleeding with clots.
Manage bladder irrigation to clear clots and give stool softeners to avoid straining.
A cancer client with fever, malaise and high WBC most likely has an infection.
c-pros-postop.source: study guide, Ch 66 and class PLQ

c-test-dx.title: Testicular cancer risk, signs and markers
points: Cryptorchidism is the greatest risk factor; the average age is 33.
The classic sign is a painless mass, sometimes with a firm or heavy feeling.
AFP and hCG should fall after the tumor is removed; if not, look for more tumor.
Cure rate is 90 to 100% if found early.

c-test-tx.title: Testicular cancer treatment and teaching
points: All types start with removal of the affected testicle (orchiectomy).
Seminoma is radiation sensitive; nonseminoma is not and gets node removal and chemotherapy.
Bank sperm before treatment; follow up for at least 10 years; retroperitoneal node removal can damage ejaculation nerves.
Bleomycin can damage the lungs and ifosfamide can cause hemorrhagic cystitis.
After surgery, hypotension with tachycardia means volume loss and fever means infection.

c-eol-diff.title: Hospice versus palliative care
points: Palliative care is for any stage of serious illness, begins at diagnosis, and can continue with curative treatment.
Hospice is for a prognosis of 6 months or less; curative treatment stops and the goal is comfort.
All hospice is palliative, but not all palliative care is hospice.

c-eol-nursing.title: Nursing care at the end of life
points: Signs death is near: falling intake and urine output, mottled cool extremities, apnea periods, noisy secretions.
Give opioids around the clock for pain and dyspnea, provide mouth care and repositioning, and honor advance directives.
Hearing is often the last sense lost.
